Psa.10.structure: Question of absence, portrait of the arrogant, the oppressed described, plea for intervention.
Psa.10.world_behind: Cursing, lying, and ambush describe real social violence in a society with weak policing and strong patronage.

deep_background.note: The psalm turns on the claim that God sees what the wicked assume he does not, an argument from character rather than circumstance.

Psa.11.occasion: A declaration of trust when the foundations themselves collapse.
Psa.11.structure: Call to flee, portrait of the archer, declaration of God's justice, vision of his face.
Psa.11.world_behind: Fleeing to the mountains was the standard refuge in times of siege, since walled cities and high ground offered safety.

deep_background.note: The phrase about foundations being destroyed points to the collapse of public order, not physical architecture.

Psa.12.occasion: A prayer for help when the faithful have disappeared from among people.
Psa.12.structure: Cry for help, portrait of flattering lips, promise of God's pure words, closing assurance.
Psa.12.world_behind: Silver refined seven times refers to metalworking practice, where repeated firing purified the metal and proved its quality.

deep_background.note: God's speech is set against human flattery, and the refining image makes the contrast about tested reliability, not mere truthfulness.

Psa.13.occasion: A fourfold 'how long' lament that ends in trust.
Psa.13.structure: Repeated questions, plea for light, request against the enemy, vow of praise.
Psa.13.world_behind: Sleeping the sleep of death and eyes growing dim were familiar signs of mortal illness, used here as the psalm's measure of danger.

deep_background.note: The psalm moves from question to vow without an answer, which is the shape most laments take in the Psalter.

Psa.14.occasion: A wisdom psalm on the fool who denies God and the corruption of humanity.
Psa.14.structure: Portrait of the fool, divine inspection, the evildoers' fear, longing for Zion's salvation.
Psa.14.world_behind: The fool in Hebrew wisdom is not intellectually slow but morally defiant, a distinction the psalm depends on.

deep_background.note: The universal claim is quoted in the New Testament, which reads the psalm as a diagnosis of humanity rather than a statistical count.

Psa.15.occasion: A question and answer about who may dwell in God's holy place.
Psa.15.structure: Entrance question, ten-part answer, promise of stability.
Psa.15.world_behind: Pilgrims arriving at the temple would be asked this at the gate, making the psalm a liturgy of entry rather than a general ethical essay.

deep_background.note: The clause describes an oath kept even at personal cost, a legal standard in a culture where a vow bound the speaker absolutely.

Psa.16.occasion: A confession of God as the only true portion and refuge.
Psa.16.structure: Plea for preservation, rejection of other gods, the boundary lines, the path of life.
Psa.16.world_behind: Boundary lines falling in pleasant places refers to land allotment, the basis of security in an agrarian society.

deep_background.note: The line about not seeing corruption is applied to resurrection in the New Testament, while in its own setting it voices unusual confidence.

Psa.17.occasion: A prayer for vindication against false accusers.
Psa.17.structure: Appeal for a fair hearing, portrait of the pursuers, request for protection, hope of waking to God's likeness.
Psa.17.world_behind: The psalm compares enemies to a lion crouching and to eyes watching, images from hunting where the ambush is decided before it begins.

deep_background.note: The image refers to the pupil, the part of the eye a person instinctively guards, and it appears again in covenant poetry.

Psa.18.occasion: A royal thanksgiving for deliverance from enemies and death.
Psa.18.structure: Declaration of love for God, distress described, theophany, rescue, reward of righteousness, victory over enemies.
Psa.18.world_behind: The theophany uses smoke, fire, darkness, and a cherub mounted on the wind, drawing on storm imagery familiar in the region.

deep_background.note: Rock, fortress, and horn are all military and topographic images, so the psalm's trust is framed in terms of defensible ground.

Psa.19.occasion: A psalm joining creation's witness to the perfection of God's law.
Psa.19.structure: Heavens declaring, the sun's course, six titles for the law, prayer for acceptable words.
Psa.19.world_behind: A bridegroom leaving his chamber and a runner's course are the two images for the sun, both from ordinary celebration and sport.

deep_background.note: Honey from the comb was the sweetest available substance, and the comparison makes the law's value a matter of taste, not duty.

Psa.20.occasion: A prayer for the king's victory before battle.
Psa.20.structure: Blessing invoked, confidence in chariots refused, final acclamation.
Psa.20.world_behind: Chariots were the decisive military technology of the age, so naming them as untrustworthy is a pointed political claim.

deep_background.note: Offerings before battle were standard practice, which is why the psalm speaks of burnt offerings and the name of God's defense.

Psa.21.occasion: Thanksgiving for the king's triumph and confidence in future victory.
Psa.21.structure: Praise for strength given, blessings described, the king's enemies addressed, closing praise.
Psa.21.world_behind: The king receiving a crown of pure gold and length of days are royal ritual images from coronation and renewal ceremonies.

deep_background.note: The psalm locates the king's stability in God's steadfast love rather than in his army, which is its political edge.

Psa.22.occasion: A lament of abandonment that turns into public praise.
Psa.22.structure: Cry of dereliction, description of suffering, plea for rescue, vow of praise in the congregation.
Psa.22.world_behind: The descriptions of pierced hands and feet, parted garments, and casting lots point to the treatment of a condemned man before a crowd.

deep_background.note: The shift to praising God among the congregation reflects Israel's public worship, where a vow was paid before witnesses.

Psa.23.occasion: A confession of God as shepherd and host.
Psa.23.structure: Shepherd provision, guidance through the valley, table and anointing, dwelling in God's house.
Psa.23.world_behind: Shepherding meant leading flocks to water and pasture and defending them at night, a task that shaped Israel's image of leadership.

deep_background.note: The rod was a club against predators and the staff a crook for guiding, so comfort here is practical protection rather than sentiment.

Psa.24.occasion: A processional psalm celebrating the LORD's entry into Zion.
Psa.24.structure: Claim of the earth for God, question of who may ascend, answer of clean hands, the King of glory entering.
Psa.24.world_behind: Processions carried the ark toward the sanctuary, and the gate dialogue reflects an actual exchange at the city doors.

deep_background.note: Addressing the gates as if they were persons is a poetic device that turns architecture into a participant in worship.

Psa.25.occasion: An acrostic prayer for guidance, forgiveness, and protection.
Psa.25.structure: Lifting the soul, request for paths, plea for pardon, confidence of covenant mercy.
Psa.25.world_behind: The alphabet structure aided memorization in a largely oral culture, so the psalm was built to be learned by heart.

deep_background.note: Intimacy with God is described as a council shared with those who fear him, an image from the royal court.

Psa.26.occasion: A prayer of integrity from one who loves God's house.
Psa.26.structure: Appeal for vindication, profession of loyalty, distance from the wicked, love of the sanctuary.
Psa.26.world_behind: Washing hands in innocence refers to the basin ritual at the altar, where priests washed before service.

deep_background.note: The flat ground of the temple court is the place of assembly, and the phrase means full participation in worship.

Psa.27.occasion: A psalm of confidence that ends in a plea for help.
Psa.27.structure: God as light and salvation, the one thing desired, prayer for guidance, call to wait.
Psa.27.world_behind: Seeking God's face and offering sacrifices with shouting were part of pilgrimage worship at the sanctuary.

deep_background.note: The phrase refers to this life rather than the grave, and it grounds the psalm's plea for rescue in the present world.

Psa.28.occasion: A plea for mercy against the wicked, ending in thanksgiving.
Psa.28.structure: Cry from the rock, request not to be dragged off with evildoers, confidence of being heard, blessing of God's people.
Psa.28.world_behind: The 'pit' and 'rock' images are drawn from cisterns and crags, both real refuges and real traps in the hill country.

deep_background.note: The king as the LORD's anointed is described as a shield for the people, so his deliverance is corporate rather than private.

Psa.29.occasion: A hymn of the voice of the LORD over the storm.
Psa.29.structure: Call to the heavenly beings, seven thunders, the LORD enthroned over the flood, blessing of strength.
Psa.29.world_behind: Cedars of Lebanon and the wilderness of Kadesh were northern and southern landmarks, so the storm sweeps the whole land and beyond.

deep_background.note: Enthroned over the flood recalls the primeval waters, placing the storm within creation order rather than outside it.

Psa.30.occasion: Thanksgiving after healing and deliverance from the grave.
Psa.30.structure: Extolling God, past cry described, the turnaround from mourning to dancing, closing vow.
Psa.30.world_behind: Turning mourning into dancing assumes the known ritual sequence of sackcloth, fasting, and celebration after deliverance.

deep_background.note: The line is built on the practice of nightlong weeping vigils that ended at daybreak, and it became one of the most quoted lines in the Psalter.

Psa.31.occasion: A prayer of trust in distress, from the psalter's most quoted laments.
Psa.31.structure: Refuge requested, distress described, plea for deliverance, praise before the congregation.
Psa.31.world_behind: 'Into your hands' is the language of entrusting a pledge or a spirit, a legal as well as a devotional act.

deep_background.note: Being like a broken pot means being discarded, an image taken from the household where cracked vessels were thrown out.

Psa.32.occasion: A wisdom psalm on the blessing of forgiveness after confession.
Psa.32.structure: Blessing of the forgiven, silence and its cost, confession and pardon, instruction to the teachable.
Psa.32.world_behind: Groaning all day and the drying of strength describe the physical toll of unconfessed guilt, understood as divine pressure.

deep_background.note: The closing warning against being like a beast controlled by bit and bridle contrasts willing obedience with brute restraint.

Psa.33.occasion: A hymn of praise for creation, providence, and the LORD's counsel.
Psa.33.structure: Call to praise, God's word and creation, the plans of nations, the eye of the LORD, closing trust.
Psa.33.world_behind: The psalm's claim that a king is not saved by a great army is a direct challenge to the military confidence of the era.

deep_background.note: Creation by speech is set against the idea of creation by combat, making the psalm's theology distinctly ordered and peaceful.

Psa.34.occasion: An acrostic thanksgiving that teaches the fear of the LORD.
Psa.34.structure: Praise before the afflicted, testimony of deliverance, instruction to children, the good life described.
Psa.34.world_behind: The psalm's promise that the young lions lack but those who seek the LORD do not is a claim about covenant provision in a subsistence economy.

deep_background.note: The invitation uses the language of eating, since a communal thanksgiving meal accompanied such a vow.

Psa.35.occasion: A lament asking God to contend against unjust accusers.
Psa.35.structure: Call to fight, description of malicious witnesses, request for vindication, vow of praise.
Psa.35.world_behind: Legal trial and military contest are blended, because the psalmist's enemies were attacking him in both court and community.

deep_background.note: Mourning dress for an enemy's illness was an act of covenant loyalty, which makes the betrayal described sharper.

Psa.36.occasion: A psalm contrasting hardened wickedness with the fountain of God's goodness.
Psa.36.structure: Portrait of the wicked, praise of steadfast love, request for protection, closing about the workers of iniquity.
Psa.36.world_behind: The image of drinking from the river of delights and sheltering under wings draws on the temple's courts and altar of refuge.

deep_background.note: Water imagery in a dry land made life visible, and the psalm uses it for the source of both light and life.

Psa.37.occasion: An acrostic wisdom psalm on fretting over the prosperous wicked.
Psa.37.structure: Fret not a sequence of instructions, the meek inheriting the land, the fate of the wicked, the righteous secured.
Psa.37.world_behind: The promise that the righteous will dwell in the land is covenant language about inherited territory, not merely prosperity.

deep_background.note: The phrase is quoted in the Sermon on the Mount, where it is applied to the kingdom rather than to property.

Psa.38.occasion: A penitential lament from a person sick and abandoned.
Psa.38.structure: Rebuke for sin, physical affliction described, abandonment by friends, confession and plea for help.
Psa.38.world_behind: The psalm's imagery of loathsome wounds echoes the skin diseases that triggered social exclusion and ritual uncleanness.

deep_background.note: The withdrawal of friends at a distance is a social fact of illness in a community where impurity spread by contact.

Psa.39.occasion: A meditation on the brevity of life and the silence of restraint.
Psa.39.structure: Guard on the mouth, silence described, the question of hope, plea for respite.
Psa.39.world_behind: Being a sojourner and a guest is legal language for someone without hereditary title to the land, applied here to every human.

deep_background.note: The hand is the smallest unit of measurement, so the psalm chooses the shortest available unit for a life span.

Psa.40.occasion: Thanksgiving for deliverance joined to a plea for help.
Psa.40.structure: Patient waiting, deliverance from the pit, new song, obedience instead of sacrifice, present distress.
Psa.40.world_behind: The pit of miry clay is a cistern, the standard well-used image for a deadly trap in a land dependent on stored water.

deep_background.note: Possibly 'ears dug out', the phrase describes the slave's willing ear as a permanent mark of obedience in Israel's law.

Psa.41.occasion: A wisdom psalm on mercy shown to the weak.
Psa.41.structure: Blessing on the merciful, plea for mercy in the speaker's own illness, betrayal by a close friend, closing blessing.
Psa.41.world_behind: Lying sick on a bed and being cursed by enemies was a public affair, since illness and reputation were bound together.

deep_background.note: Sharing bread at the table created real obligation, which is why the betrayal described is a covenant offense.

Psa.51.occasion: David's prayer after Nathan confronted him over Bathsheba.
Psa.51.structure: Plea for mercy, confession of sin, request for a clean heart, vow of praise.
Psa.51.world_behind: Sin is framed as offence against God first, in a world where sacrifice was the normal remedy; the psalm insists a broken spirit outranks ritual.

deep_background.note: Hyssop was the brush used to sprinkle cleansing water and blood, tying the plea to leper and altar cleansing rites.

Psa.52.occasion: A wisdom psalm against a boastful man of violence.
Psa.52.structure: Indictment of the tyrant's tongue, his coming ruin, the righteous looking on, the psalmist like a green olive.
Psa.52.world_behind: Reputation and the tongue carried real social power in a village economy; slander could destroy a household's standing.

deep_background.note: Olives live for centuries and regrow from the stump, a standard image of enduring vitality in the house of God.

Psa.53.occasion: A wisdom lament over universal corruption, a variant of Psalm 14.
Psa.53.structure: The fool's denial, God's inspection of humanity, dread of the righteous, longing for Zion's salvation.
Psa.53.world_behind: Denial of God here is not philosophical atheism but practical disregard, treating life as unaccountable.

deep_background.note: The claim is corporate rather than individual, describing a society that has abandoned covenant loyalty.

Psa.54.occasion: Prayer when betrayed to Saul by the Ziphites.
Psa.54.structure: Appeal for deliverance, description of hostile strangers, confidence of God's help, freewill offering.
Psa.54.world_behind: The Ziphites lived in the Judean wilderness and gained by currying favour with the king, so betrayal had an economic edge.

deep_background.note: A voluntary sacrifice beyond what the law required, given as thanksgiving rather than obligation.

Psa.55.occasion: A lament from the city under threat, betrayed by a close companion.
Psa.55.structure: Anguish and longing for wings, the city's violence, the traitor named, a call for judgment, closing trust.
Psa.55.world_behind: The psalm describes an ancient walled city where night patrols and factional violence made streets unsafe.

deep_background.note: The idiom means to hand a load to someone else; the LORD is pictured as the one who sustains the pack.

Psa.56.occasion: Prayer when seized by Philistines at Gath.
Psa.56.structure: Plea for mercy, enemies described, trust refrain repeated, praise and thanksgiving.
Psa.56.world_behind: A captured man at Gath had no legal standing, so the psalm's trust is the plea of someone with no patron.

deep_background.note: Ancient mourners collected tears in small flasks, and the image says God keeps a record of every grief.

Psa.57.occasion: Prayer in a cave while hunted, traditionally David fleeing Saul.
Psa.57.structure: Refuge under wings, enemies as lions, exaltation refrain, awakening to praise at dawn.
Psa.57.world_behind: Caves in the Judean hills served as shelters and hideouts for outlaws and fugitives.

deep_background.note: The psalm addresses its own inner being, calling the whole self to praise before daybreak.

Psa.58.occasion: A protest against unjust judges and rulers.
Psa.58.structure: Rebuke of silent judges, portrait of the wicked as venomous, imprecation for their defeat, confidence the righteous are rewarded.
Psa.58.world_behind: Judges sat at city gates and were expected to protect the poor; taking bribes was a persistent prophetic complaint.

deep_background.note: Rulers are addressed as divine appointees, drawing on the idea that human judges act in God's place.

Psa.59.occasion: Prayer when Saul sent men to watch the house.
Psa.59.structure: Deliverance plea, the attackers likened to dogs, judgment on the nations, strength refrain, morning praise.
Psa.59.world_behind: A stakeout of a private house needed only a few men, and city homes had windows overlooking narrow streets.

deep_background.note: Scavenging dogs roamed ancient streets at night, a common image of threat and contempt.

Psa.60.occasion: A national lament after a military defeat, remembered against Edom.
Psa.60.structure: God's anger described, the land shaken, a call to restore, an oracle of triumph, help against the foe.
Psa.60.world_behind: Edom and Israel fought repeatedly over the trade routes south of the Dead Sea.

deep_background.note: Two sites either side of the Jordan, used to claim God's rule over the whole land.

Psa.61.occasion: Prayer from distance or exile for the king's stability.
Psa.61.structure: Cry from the ends of the earth, the rock higher than I, a vow to dwell in God's tent, prayer for the king.
Psa.61.world_behind: Kingship was bound to the temple and capital, so a prayer for the king's long reign was a prayer for national security.

deep_background.note: The image comes from the cherubim whose wings overshadowed the ark, the place of asylum.

Psa.62.occasion: A quiet psalm of trust in the face of threat.
Psa.62.structure: Rest in God alone, enemies like a leaning wall, repeated refrain of trust, a warning against trusting wealth.
Psa.62.world_behind: Wealth was measured in weighed silver and produce; the psalm targets the confidence money creates.

deep_background.note: Weighing silver with dishonest scales printed on the palm was an image of social injustice.

Psa.63.occasion: Prayer from the wilderness of Judah, thirsting for God.
Psa.63.structure: Thirst, vision of God in the sanctuary, praise at night, enemies doomed, the king rejoices.
Psa.63.world_behind: The Judean desert east of Jerusalem is rainless for months; water and shade were literally life.

deep_background.note: Fat and marrow meant the best portion of a sacrifice, the feast that followed worship.

Psa.64.occasion: A lament against hidden conspiracy and slander.
Psa.64.structure: Plea for protection, the plotters described with weapons as words, sudden divine judgment, the upright glad.
Psa.64.world_behind: Politics at court ran on whispers and alliances; a formed conspiracy could end a career or a life.

deep_background.note: Speech is pictured as a weapon in ancient wisdom as regularly as the bow or arrow.

Psa.65.occasion: A harvest thanksgiving, God praised for forgiveness and provision.
Psa.65.structure: Praise in Zion, the God who hears prayer, the God of the harvest, the waters and fields shouting for joy.
Psa.65.world_behind: Israel depended on autumn and spring rains; the harvest festivals thanked God for water as much as for grain.

deep_background.note: Rain is described falling on ploughed furrows, an image of abundance soaking the earth.

Psa.66.occasion: A communal thanksgiving after deliverance, with vows paid in the temple.
Psa.66.structure: Call to praise, God's testing described, the psalmist's testimony, vows paid, a call for all who fear God to listen.
Psa.66.world_behind: Vows made in danger were fulfilled publicly at the sanctuary, often with a shared meal.

deep_background.note: Standard covenant imagery for severe trial, later echoing in Isaiah and in the church's language of testing.

Psa.67.occasion: A prayer for blessing that the nations may know God.
Psa.67.structure: Prayer for the shining face, the purpose of blessing the nations, the earth's yield, a closing refrain.
Psa.67.world_behind: The Aaronic blessing was spoken over the people at the sanctuary, so the psalm adapts a priestly formula for mission.

deep_background.note: The face shining means granting favour, the opposite of hiding the face, which means withholding it.

Psa.68.occasion: A processional psalm of God's march from Sinai to Zion.
Psa.68.structure: God rises, the wilderness procession, Sinai and the divine army, Zion as God's dwelling, a worldwide kingdom, praise.
Psa.68.world_behind: Processions with the ark moved through the hills from former sanctuaries to the capital, dramatising conquest.

deep_background.note: Bashan in the north was horse-and-chariot country, so its mention pictures the strongest military power yielding.

Psa.69.occasion: A lament of an innocent sufferer, widely quoted in the Gospels.
Psa.69.structure: The deep waters, hostility for zeal, shame and rejection, imprecation, a plea for salvation, praise that pleases God.
Psa.69.world_behind: The psalm's sufferer is mocked in public, the place where honour and shame were decided.

deep_background.note: The line is applied to Jesus cleansing the temple, linking worship disorder with contempt for the sufferer.

Psa.70.occasion: An urgent prayer for deliverance, nearly identical to Psalm 40's close.
Psa.70.structure: Petition for rescue, imprecation on enemies, a closing shout that God is great and mindful of the poor.
Psa.70.world_behind: Ancient courts offered no help to the poor, so appeals for justice had to be addressed to God directly.

deep_background.note: The taunt sound mimics public mockery, the same word used of enemies gloating in other laments.

Psa.71.occasion: The prayer of an aged believer facing decline and enemies.
Psa.71.structure: Refuge plea, God as hope from youth, plea not to be cast off in old age, confidence in God's righteousness, vow of praise.
Psa.71.world_behind: Elders held honour in Israelite society, but a frail old man without protectors was vulnerable to those who coveted his land.

deep_background.note: The psalm claims lifelong belonging to God, the language of a servant born into a household.

Psa.72.occasion: A royal psalm for a king's reign and the close of Book II.
Psa.72.structure: Prayer for justice, the king as rain on mown grass, universal dominion, deliverance for the needy, a doxology.
Psa.72.world_behind: Ancient kings were judged by whether the poor received justice at the gate, so royal prayers were public policy in liturgical form.

deep_background.note: Sheba's incense and gold trade made it the emblem of the farthest wealth the king should attract.

Psa.73.occasion: A wisdom psalm wrestling with the prosperity of the wicked.
Psa.73.structure: Confession of near-stumbling, portrait of the prosperous wicked, the turn in the sanctuary, the end of the wicked, nearness to God.
Psa.73.world_behind: The sanctuary visit recalls a temple encounter where the eyes of faith were corrected, not a philosophical argument.

deep_background.note: The image comes from mountain tracks in Judea, where a settled stone could send a traveller down a slope.

Psa.74.occasion: A communal lament over a destroyed sanctuary, likely after 586 BC.
Psa.74.structure: Why has God rejected, the enemy in the sanctuary, recount of God's creation power, a plea for the covenant.
Psa.74.world_behind: The Babylonian sack of Jerusalem burned the temple and removed its vessels, ending the sacrificial system.

deep_background.note: Refers to the loss of the temple's prophetic and cultic signals, not simply to the sun and stars.

Psa.75.occasion: A thanksgiving psalm affirming God's timing in judgment.
Psa.75.structure: Praise that God's name is near, a divine oracle on timing, the cup of judgment, horns lifted and cut off.
Psa.75.world_behind: A raised horn is an animal's display of strength, so lifting a horn became the idiom for asserting power.

deep_background.note: Mixed wine in God's hand is a fixed biblical image for a portion of wrath poured out for the world to drink.

Psa.76.occasion: A Zion psalm celebrating God's victory over the enemy.
Psa.76.structure: God known in Judah, the breaking of weapons, the God who judges, the earth's silence, vows and gifts.
Psa.76.world_behind: Jerusalem's survival against Assyria in 701 BC shaped the confidence that God defends the city in person.

deep_background.concept: Both horse and chariot lie still
deep_background.note: Chariots were the tanks of the ancient world, so their stillness means total military collapse.

Psa.77.occasion: A night lament that turns to memory of God's mighty acts.
Psa.77.structure: Cry in trouble, sleepless reflection, questions of God's faithfulness, remembering the deeds at the sea.
Psa.77.world_behind: Night was a time of real danger and bad news could not travel until morning, so sleeplessness was a natural setting for lament.

deep_background.concept: Right hand of the Most High
deep_background.note: The right hand was the hand of strength and oath, the image of God acting decisively.

Psa.78.occasion: A historical psalm rehearsing Israel's rebellion and God's patience.
Psa.78.structure: Call to hear a lesson, Ephraim's failure, wilderness rebellion and provision, the plagues, the rejection of Shiloh, the choice of Judah and David.
Psa.78.world_behind: Teaching was transmitted orally in households, so the psalm enacts what it commands: telling the next generation.

deep_background.note: The earlier sanctuary where the ark was lost to the Philistines, used here as a warning that no place is safe without obedience.

Psa.79.occasion: A lament over a defiled city and a plea for God's name's sake.
Psa.79.structure: Nations invade the inheritance, the psalmist's plea, forgiveness sought, sevenfold repayment, a final vow.
Psa.79.world_behind: To defile a sanctuary was to conquer its god; the psalm argues that God's honour is at stake, not just Israel's pride.

deep_background.note: Siege warfare left the dead unburied, a horror that meant the bodies could not rest and the land was polluted.

Psa.80.occasion: A prayer for restoration after national harm, with the vine image.
Psa.80.structure: Shepherd plea, refrain to restore, the vine brought from Egypt and now broken down, plea for the man at God's right hand.
Psa.80.world_behind: Vineyards were cleared by burning and broke under boar and armies, so a ruined vineyard was a vivid picture of invasion.

deep_background.note: Wild boar roamed Judean woodland and devastated crops, a natural picture of a pagan aggressor.

Psa.81.occasion: A festival psalm with a divine oracle calling Israel to listen.
Psa.81.structure: Call to sing at the feast, the oracle recalling the exodus, the conditional promise, the lament that Israel would not listen.
Psa.81.world_behind: Feasts required music and sacrifice, and the trumpet on the new moon marked the calendar's holy days.

deep_background.concept: A law for the God of Jacob
deep_background.note: The psalm ties festal observance to covenant obligation rather than mere ritual celebration.

Psa.82.occasion: A vision of God judging the judges.
Psa.82.structure: God takes his place in the council, indicts partial judges, revocation of their divine status, a call for God to judge the earth.
Psa.82.world_behind: Justice was administered at city gates by elders and officials, often swayed by bribes and by the status of the parties.

deep_background.note: The line is cited in John's Gospel to show that God's word was given to those who represent him.

Psa.83.occasion: A national lament over a coalition against Israel.
Psa.83.structure: List of conspirators, comparison to past defeats, prayer for them to know God alone.
Psa.83.world_behind: An alliance of Edom, Moab, Amalek, Philistia and Tyre would threaten the eastern frontiers of Israel.

deep_background.note: Acknowledging the name meant recognising a nation's god; the prayer asks for defeat so the hostile nations recognise the LORD.

Psa.84.occasion: The song of a pilgrim longing for the courts of God.
Psa.84.structure: How lovely is your dwelling, longing of the soul, the pilgrimage through the valley of weeping, one day in the courts, the pilgrim's blessing.
Psa.84.world_behind: Pilgrims travelled on foot to Jerusalem for the annual feasts, passing dry ravines that could flood in winter rains.

deep_background.note: A dry desert crossing the psalm turns into springs, an image of the road itself becoming a place of refreshing.

Psa.85.occasion: A prayer for revival after forgiven judgment.
Psa.85.structure: Recollection of past grace, plea for restoration, the oracle of peace, love and faithfulness meeting.
Psa.85.world_behind: National revival at that period meant renewed harvests, safety on the roads and the return of festival worship.

deep_background.note: Personified virtues meeting is a poetic way of describing a restored relationship between God's justice and his mercy.

Psa.86.occasion: A personal prayer for teaching and protection, the only Davidic psalm in Book III.
Psa.86.structure: Plea for hearing, God's goodness, the nations coming to worship, a single heart, the pit of Sheol, a plea for help.
Psa.86.world_behind: Sheol meant the grave, a place of silence where the dead could not praise God, so death ended the psalmist's worship.

deep_background.note: Ancient patrons displayed favour publicly, so the psalm asks for a visible vindication before his enemies.

Psa.87.occasion: A psalm celebrating Zion as the mother city of all nations.
Psa.87.structure: God's foundation on the holy mountains, the nations registered in Zion, springs within her.
Psa.87.world_behind: Birth records of citizens were kept by cities, so being registered in Zion was a claim to full belonging.

deep_background.note: Rahab is a nickname for Egypt; pairing it with Babylon names Israel's two great oppressors as future citizens of Zion.

Psa.88.occasion: The darkest lament in the psalter, from a sufferer near death.
Psa.88.structure: Cry by day and night, the pit and the grave, God's wrath described, affliction from youth, the final plea in darkness.
Psa.88.world_behind: Illness and dying were understood as conditions of ritual uncleanness, so the sick often lived at society's edge.

deep_background.note: The psalm ends without a resolution verse, which is why the church has used it for Good Friday.

Psa.89.occasion: A royal lament in which the Davidic covenant appears broken.
Psa.89.structure: Praise of God's steadfast love, the covenant with David, the promise, the lament that God has cast off his anointed, a closing plea.
Psa.89.world_behind: The covenant with David was the theological foundation of the monarchy, so a military defeat raised a crisis about God's word.

deep_background.note: Fixed calendar signs were called on as legal witnesses, and the moon in particular marked monthly festal time.

Psa.90.occasion: A prayer of Moses on human frailty and God's eternity.
Psa.90.structure: God's dwelling before the mountains, the thousand years, the flood of time, a plea to return, teach us to number our days, establish the work of our hands.
Psa.90.world_behind: Life expectancy in the ancient world was low, and the psalm's seventy years fit the realities of disease and war.

deep_background.note: Counting days is an accounting metaphor, seeking a heart that calculates worth rather than merely counting.

Psa.91.occasion: A psalm of protection for one who shelters in God.
Psa.91.structure: Dwelling in the shelter, dangers enumerated, angels marshalled, the divine promise of protection and long life.
Psa.91.world_behind: Travellers feared plague, night attack, arrows and wild beasts, all of which the psalm lists as a timetable of danger.

deep_background.note: Shade meant protection in a hot land, and the divine name El Shaddai evokes the mountain's shelter.

Psa.92.structure: Good to give thanks, the wicked as grass that withers, the righteous as palms and cedars, old age still fruitful.
Psa.92.world_behind: Palms and cedars were planted in temple courts, where the psalm's worshippers would have stood among them.

deep_background.concept: Planted in the house of the LORD
deep_background.note: Temple courts were planted gardens, so flourishing for the righteous was literally pictured by the courtyard trees.

Psa.93.occasion: A short hymn declaring the LORD's reign.
Psa.93.structure: The LORD robes himself in majesty, the floods lift their voices, God is mightier, God's decrees stand.
Psa.93.world_behind: The sea and flood waters were the primeval symbol of chaos, so the psalm's claim is that God rules the untameable.

deep_background.note: Royal accession was marked by robing, so the psalm uses coronation imagery for creation itself.

Psa.94.occasion: A communal lament asking God to punish the proud.
Psa.94.structure: Appeal for vengeance, indictment of oppression of widows and strangers, the psalmist's consolation, God as refuge.
Psa.94.world_behind: Widows, foreigners and orphans had no land or male protector, the three groups the law repeatedly commands Israel to defend.

deep_background.note: The phrase suggests a court that uses law to legalise harm, a judicial system turned against the poor.

Psa.95.occasion: A processional call to worship with a warning.
Psa.95.structure: Sing and shout to the rock of salvation, God as maker and shepherd, the warning at Meribah.
Psa.95.world_behind: Meribah was the wilderness site where Israel tested God for water, a memory carried in the pilgrimage route.

deep_background.note: The wilderness generation's failure becomes a liturgical warning each year at the harvest feast.

Psa.96.occasion: A new song of God's universal kingship.
Psa.96.structure: Sing a new song, declare his glory among the nations, the LORD above all gods, let creation rejoice, judgment is coming.
Psa.96.world_behind: Nations measured power by gods, so proclaiming a god's glory among the nations was a political claim as much as a religious one.

deep_background.note: Pitched against creation myths in which the world is unstable and re-fought each year, the psalm says the created order holds.

Psa.97.occasion: A hymn of divine reign and judgment.
Psa.97.structure: The LORD reigns, clouds and fire, the mountains melt, idols put to shame, light is sown for the righteous.
Psa.97.world_behind: Thunderous storm imagery was the standard language for a god's arrival, drawn from ancient Near Eastern battle hymns.

deep_background.note: Seed imagery says hope is planted in darkness and grows later, not that it disappears.

Psa.98.occasion: A new song celebrating God's salvation and coming judgment.
Psa.98.structure: Sing a new song, his right arm revealed, the nations see salvation, creation breaks into song, judgment announced.
Psa.98.world_behind: Victory announcements were made in the temple and spread by singers, which is the psalm's own function.

deep_background.note: Personifying rivers echoes ancient poetry where creation celebrates divine victory, as in Egyptian and Mesopotamian hymns.

Psa.99.occasion: A Zion hymn of God's holiness.
Psa.99.structure: The LORD reigns, exalted above the cherubim, the king loves justice, Moses and Aaron called on him, worship at his footstool.
Psa.99.world_behind: The ark's cherubim throne and the pillar of cloud were the visible signs of God's presence in the temple.

deep_background.note: Calling the earthly throne a footstool kept the ark subordinate to God's heavenly rule, guarding against idolatry.

Psa.100.occasion: A short processional hymn of praise at the temple gates.
Psa.100.structure: Shout for joy, serve with gladness, know he made us, enter his gates with thanksgiving, his love endures.
Psa.100.world_behind: Gates and courts had thresholds with symbolic protection, and worshippers entered with sacrifice in hand.

deep_background.note: The pastoral image joins two metaphors, God as shepherd and God as owner of the land.

Psa.101.occasion: A ruler's psalm on household integrity.
Psa.101.structure: Purpose to sing of love and justice, aim at a blameless way, opposition to the wicked, servants of the faithful.
Psa.101.world_behind: A king's court staffed his household, so choosing who stayed in the home was a real political and integrity act.

deep_background.note: Judgment is portrayed as daily household management, not a final court session.

Psa.102.occasion: The prayer of an afflicted person, casting hope on Zion's future.
Psa.102.structure: Lament in frailty, the days of Zion remembered and rebuilt, the nations will fear, prayer of the destitute recorded, heavens will perish.
Psa.102.world_behind: Writing a prayer down and preserving it served as a legal record of an appeal, the practice the psalm claims God follows.

deep_background.concept: He regards the prayer of the destitute
deep_background.note: Fasting and cape-shafted sackcloth made a person socially invisible in ancient cities.

Psa.103.occasion: A psalm of blessing and thanksgiving.
Psa.103.structure: Bless the LORD, forget not his benefits, forgiveness and renewal, God's compassion as a father, human frailty, renewed call to praise.
Psa.103.world_behind: The word for benefits covers both gifts and a servant's due; the psalm list reads as a household accounts statement.

deep_background.note: The Hebrew word can mean the bird of prey or a lantern, either image meaning that life is quickly gone.

Psa.104.structure: The LORD clothed in light, creation ordered, water and plants, creatures all fed, the sea and Leviathan, praise and repentance.
Psa.104.world_behind: Creation language draws on imagery shared with Egyptian and Canaanite hymns, adapted to one Creator with no rival.

deep_background.note: Leviathan usually stands for chaos, so making it a playful creature says chaos itself obeys God's delight.

Psa.105.structure: Give thanks, God's oath to Abraham, Joseph in Egypt, Moses and the plagues, the exodus and settlement.
Psa.105.world_behind: Covenant memory in Israel included concrete promises of land, not merely ideas, so the poem recounts geography.

deep_background.concept: He rebuked kings for their sake
deep_background.note: Recalls the safety of the patriarchs under foreign rulers, a claim of God's protection without an army.

Psa.106.occasion: A communal confession of Israel's repeated rebellion.
Psa.106.structure: Praise and petition, the exodus rebellion, the golden calf, the wilderness generation, the settlement's compromise, a closing save and gather.
Psa.106.world_behind: This psalm sits at the boundary of the exile, when Israel's failure was read through the lens of covenant curses.

deep_background.note: The circumcised and defended covenant is praised as the model for a threatened people.

Psa.107.occasion: A thanksgiving psalm with four pictures of redemption.
Psa.107.structure: Call for the redeemed to speak, wanderers in desert, prisoners in chains, the sick, the storm at sea, and a closing call to the wise.
Psa.107.world_behind: Four classic images of ancient catastrophe, travel through dry land, imprisonment, illness and sea peril.

deep_background.note: Sea storms were feared as living chaos, and travellers offered sacrifice on landing out of genuine terror.

Psa.108.occasion: A psalm of confidence blending praise with war prayer.
Psa.108.structure: Awake my heart, praise among the nations, God will triumph, an oracle of conquest, help against the enemy.
Psa.108.world_behind: The psalm reuses material from earlier collections, showing how the temple's singers edited and recombined old poems.

deep_background.note: Also in Psalm 60, the pair represents east and west of the Jordan, i.e. total claim to the land.

Psa.109.occasion: A fierce lament against false accusers.
Psa.109.structure: Plea for intervention, curses on the accuser, the psalmist's frailty described, a closing appeal for God's name's sake.
Psa.109.world_behind: In an honour-shame culture, public accusation could ruin a family for a season and a name through generations.

deep_background.note: The psalm hands the enemy over to God's judgment and refuses personal vengeance, the interpretive key the church used.

Psa.110.occasion: A royal psalm of the king and priest to come.
Psa.110.structure: Oracle of sitting at God's right hand, the staff of rule, the priest forever in Melchizedek's order, the judgment of nations, the king's victory.
Psa.110.world_behind: Melchizedek made sacrifice uninherited; the psalm claims a lasting priestly line outside the Levitical structure.

deep_background.note: To sit at a king's right hand was to share the throne and the rule, the basis for later messianic claims.

Psa.111.occasion: A praise psalm in acrostic form.
Psa.111.structure: Praise in the assembly, God's works and covenant, the fear of the LORD as the beginning of wisdom.
Psa.111.world_behind: The acrostic pattern was a teaching device, and the psalm's regular rhythm demanded memorisation.

deep_background.note: Wisdom here begins with awe at God's covenant faithfulness, not with intellectual information.

Psa.112.occasion: A wisdom psalm on the blessed household.
Psa.112.structure: Blessed is the one who fears the LORD, prosperity for children, generosity to the poor, security without fear.
Psa.112.world_behind: Despite the conventional language of the prosperous household, the psalm explicitly ties blessing to lending generously.

deep_background.note: Interest-bearing loans were forbidden within the community, so the righteous lend without extracting interest.

Psa.113.occasion: A festival hymn of God's condescension.
Psa.113.structure: Praise his name, God above the heavens, he stoops to look, he raises the poor, he settles the barren in a home.
Psa.113.world_behind: The psalm stands opposite Psalm 112, celebrating not prosperity but God's choice of the lowly.

deep_background.note: Childlessness carried social death in Israel, so this promise works as a form of implied resurrection.

Psa.114.occasion: A short hymn of the exodus.
Psa.114.structure: Judah became God's sanctuary, the sea fled, the mountains skipped, the earth trembles at God's presence, water from the rock.
Psa.114.world_behind: The sea and the mountains are the two great barriers to travel; both yield, so no obstacle remains.

deep_background.note: Hills were thought of as ancient and immovable, so their dancing is an image of creation recognising its master.

Psa.115.occasion: A psalm of trust answering the mockery of idolaters.
Psa.115.structure: Not to us but to your name, the heathen gods, Israel is to trust, the LORD blesses those who fear him, the dead do not praise.
Psa.115.world_behind: Idol polemic is common in exilic and post-exilic texts where Israel lived among imperial cults.

deep_background.note: The satire follows a fixed formula on religious images, contrasting lifeless metal with the living God.

Psa.116.occasion: A personal thanksgiving for rescue from death.
Psa.116.structure: Love the LORD for hearing me, the snares of death, God's grace, rest of my soul, walking before the LORD in the land of the living.
Psa.116.world_behind: The grave was the boundary that cancelled temple participation, so being spared meant being able to worship again.

deep_background.concept: Precious in the sight of the LORD
deep_background.note: The price of a life was measured in silver; the psalm says God values the saint's death at far more.

Psa.117.occasion: A two-verse call for all nations to praise the LORD.
Psa.117.structure: Praise him, all nations; his love is strong, the faithfulness of the LORD endures forever.
Psa.117.world_behind: The shortest chapter is deliberately universal, using the same phrase later quoted in Romans 15.

deep_background.note: In a period of restrictive national faith, the psalm is openly international, part of the tradition of mission inherent in the covenant.

Psa.118.occasion: A festival thanksgiving, the last of the Hallel psalms.
Psa.118.structure: Give thanks, his love endures, the distress narrative, the LORD is my strength, the stone the builders rejected, a festal procession and blessing.
Psa.118.world_behind: The two choirs, one inside and one outside the gate, alternated lines as the procession arrived.

deep_background.note: Builders slotted rough-cut stones by match, so a rejected block became a corner capital, an image applied to the rejected king.

Psa.119.occasion: The great acrostic psalm on God's word.
Psa.119.structure: Twenty-two stanzas, one per Hebrew letter, circling the law, the way, testimony, precept, command and promise.
Psa.119.world_behind: Acrostic structure is a testimony of completeness, the whole alphabet of devotion, likely used for teaching.

deep_background.note: Travel was done at night with a small clay lamp, so the image is practical, describing safe steps rather than general illumination.

Psa.120.occasion: The first song of ascents, from a traveller in a distant land.
Psa.120.structure: Distress over lying lips, a warrior's arrows, a lament at dwelling in Meshech, a wish for peace.
Psa.120.world_behind: The songs of ascents were sung by pilgrims on the road up to Jerusalem for the three annual feasts.

deep_background.note: Naming these distant peoples puts the singer among foreigners, the condition of diaspora.

Psa.121.occasion: A pilgrim song of confidence on the road.
Psa.121.structure: Lift my eyes to the hills, help from the LORD, he does not slumber, he keeps you night and day, he guards your going out and coming in.
Psa.121.world_behind: Jerusalem sits among hills and travellers passed through valleys where robbers and heat waited, so the psalm's watchfulness is physical.

deep_background.note: Desert sun could kill, so shade meant life; the LORD as shade is a practical picture of unbroken protection.

Psa.122.occasion: A pilgrim's joy at arriving in Jerusalem.
Psa.122.structure: Gladness at going to the house of the LORD, the city compact together, the thrones of judgment, prayer for peace.
Psa.122.world_behind: The tribes came up for festivals, and the city's gates and walls were the visible proof of security and justice.

deep_background.concept: The seats of the house of David
deep_background.note: Gate chambers served as courts, so the psalm links worship with the places where cases were decided.

Psa.123.occasion: A short communal plea for mercy under contempt.
Psa.123.structure: Eyes lifted to the LORD, waiting for mercy, the contempt of the proud and the scoffing of the wealthy.
Psa.123.world_behind: Ancient legal and social standing depended on patrons, so a community mocked by the wealthy had few ways to recover honour.

deep_background.note: Servants watched a master's hand for orders, so waiting on God is described with the everyday posture of service.

Psa.124.occasion: A national thanksgiving for narrow escape.
Psa.124.structure: Had not the LORD been with us, the flood would have swallowed us, the snare is broken, our help is in his name.
Psa.124.world_behind: The psalter images national peril as a flood and a bird trap, two everyday dangers in the ancient world.

deep_background.note: Fowlers caught small birds with nets and snares; the image gives thanks for an escape nobody engineered.

Psa.125.occasion: A psalm of trust in God's protection of Zion.
Psa.125.structure: As the mountains surround Jerusalem, the LORD surrounds his people, the sceptre of wickedness will not rest there, peace on Israel.
Psa.125.world_behind: Jerusalem's geography, ringed by steeper ridges, was itself a defensive picture the psalmist could point to.

deep_background.note: The word for staff here is the rod of an overlord, meaning imperial rule that lays claim to the community's land.

Psa.126.occasion: Thanksgiving after the return from exile.
Psa.126.structure: The LORD restored Zion, mouths filled with laughter, the nations recognised the deed, prayer to restore again, tears become songs of harvest.
Psa.126.world_behind: Returning exiles resettled ruined towns, and the first harvest seasons were the real proof of restoration.

deep_background.note: The Negev's dry washes fill suddenly in winter rain; the image is of joy arriving without slow buildup.

Psa.127.occasion: A wisdom psalm on dependence and family.
Psa.127.structure: Unless the LORD builds the house, waking in vain, the beloved sleeps, children as a heritage and arrows.
Psa.127.world_behind: House construction was a community labour done stone by stone, so the psalm's image of vain labour was concrete.

deep_background.note: Households relied on sons for defence in a society without standing police or armies.

Psa.128.occasion: A wisdom psalm on the blessed household.
Psa.128.structure: Blessed are all who fear the LORD, you will eat from your hands' work, your wife as a fruitful vine, children like olive shoots, peace on Israel.
Psa.128.world_behind: Vine and olive were the two staple crops, each needing years of investment, so their fruit meant security.

deep_background.note: A shared meal at one's own table was the picture of a settled household, contrasted with a wandering or exiled life.

Psa.129.occasion: A communal psalm recalling affliction since youth.
Psa.129.structure: Much have they afflicted me, the ploughmen on my back, the LORD is righteous and has cut the cords, a curse on those who hate Zion.
Psa.129.world_behind: A Hebrew slave could be beaten to a drawn mark with a rod, of which the plough furrow is a deliberate image.

deep_background.note: Flat roofs collected dust where grass sprouted and died early, an image of hope without substance.

Psa.130.occasion: A penitential song of ascent from the depths.
Psa.130.structure: Out of the depths I cry, forgiveness with you that you may be feared, the soul waits more than watchmen, redemption promised.
Psa.130.world_behind: Watchmen spent the night on city walls waiting for dawn, the standard image for endured hope.

deep_background.note: The depths evoke both sea chaos and the grave, the two places a person cannot reach out from.

Psa.131.occasion: A short psalm of quiet trust.
Psa.131.structure: My heart is not lifted up, my eyes are not proud, I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child, hope in the LORD forever.
Psa.131.world_behind: The image of a weaned child depends on the long nursing period of the ancient household, where the child then joins family discipline.

deep_background.note: The child is no longer demanding milk, so the picture is contentment that has finished with grasping.

Psa.132.occasion: A royal psalm recalling David's oath and the ark's move to Zion.
Psa.132.structure: Remember David's hardships, the oath to find a place for the LORD, the journey of the ark, the divine answer with blessing on priests and people.
Psa.132.world_behind: David's capture of Jerusalem gave him a neutral capital that he inserted the ark into, turning it into a national sanctuary.

deep_background.note: The temple was called a resting place rather than a dwelling, emphasizing God's choice rather than human need.

Psa.133.occasion: A short song of ascent on unity.
Psa.133.structure: How good and pleasant brothers dwell together, oil from Aaron's beard, dew of Hermon on Zion, life forevermore.
Psa.133.world_behind: Crowds lodging together in the city during feast days made unity a practical issue rather than an idea.

deep_background.note: The oil used for priests and the tabernacle was made from a guarded recipe and could not be imitated for ordinary use.

Psa.134.occasion: The final song of ascent, blessing for the night watch.
Psa.134.structure: Bless the LORD all you servants in the house by night, lift holy hands, the LORD bless you from Zion.
Psa.134.world_behind: Levites kept night vigils at the sanctuary to maintain fire and order, so a song addressing them fits a real roster.

deep_background.note: The hands of a priest had to be ritually clean, the gesture of a permitted approach to the altar.

Psa.135.occasion: A communal praise psalm on God's works.
Psa.135.structure: Praise the name, God's choice of Jacob, the LORD is above all gods, the works of creation, the exodus, the conquest, the futility of idols.
Psa.135.world_behind: The psalm borrows language from the exodus and conquest traditions, using them as public memory.

deep_background.note: A memorial name was invoked to keep a bond alive, the way treaties were recited to make them binding.

Psa.136.occasion: An antiphonal thanksgiving at the temple.
Psa.136.structure: Give thanks, his love endures forever, repeated after each line through creation, exodus, conquest and providence.
Psa.136.world_behind: Responsive reading trained a crowd that mostly could not read; the refrain let everyone participate with one memorised line.

deep_background.note: The Hebrew word is the covenant word for steadfast love, the character declared at Sinai and echoed in every stanza.

Psa.137.occasion: A lament of exiles in Babylon after the destruction of Jerusalem.
Psa.137.structure: By the rivers of Babylon, harps hung on willows, the taunt of captors, lament of memory, a demand for judgment on Edom and Babylon.
Psa.137.world_behind: Deportation was an imperial policy that moved artisans and scribes to the capital to serve the empire.

deep_background.note: Babylon's irrigation canals stood in for the waters of a temple liturgy, so worship began in a foreign land.

Psa.138.occasion: A personal thanksgiving for God's answer and protection.
Psa.138.structure: I give you thanks with my whole heart, praise before the gods, the day I called you answered, the LORD regards the lowly, he will fulfill his purpose.
Psa.138.world_behind: Proclaiming God's name before kings and their pantheons was a public act with potential legal consequences.

deep_background.note: God's attention to the lowly is a recurrent claim in the psalter, contrasting with court patronage systems.

Psa.139.occasion: A psalm on God's intimate knowledge of the psalmist.
Psa.139.structure: You have searched me, you know my rising and sitting, you surround me, where can I flee, formed in the womb, search me and know my heart.
Psa.139.world_behind: The psalm's anatomy language belongs to a world where the heart was the mind and the kidneys the seat of feeling.

deep_background.note: A heavenly register records the psalmist's days, the same image used elsewhere for the register of the living.

Psa.140.occasion: A lament against violent and powerful adversaries.
Psa.140.structure: Deliver me from evil men, their tongues like serpents, a plea for God's protection, a prayer that their plans fail, a closing confidence.
Psa.140.world_behind: The psalm's picture of the poor is one whose case is not heard at court because the rich control it.

deep_background.note: The imagery draws on the desert viper, a creature that needed no provocation to kill.

Psa.141.occasion: An evening prayer for restraint and protection.
Psa.141.structure: I call to you, let my prayer be incense, set a guard over my mouth, let the righteous rebuke me, a plea for escape from traps.
Psa.141.world_behind: Evening incense was offered at the temple altar, so the psalm's worshipper defers to a full liturgy.

deep_background.note: Incense accompanied sacrifice in the temple courts, and the psalms explicitly replace sacrifice with prayer in the exile and after.

Psa.142.occasion: A prayer from a cave, a maskil of David.
Psa.142.structure: I cry with my voice, no one cares for me, my refuge is in you, deliver me from prison that I may praise.
Psa.142.world_behind: A cave in the Judean wilderness was a hideout, not a place anyone could be found, so the psalm's loneliness is geographic.

deep_background.concept: My portion in the land of the living
deep_background.note: Covenant language for an allotment, applied to the psalmist's life itself when land and safety are denied.

Psa.143.occasion: A penitential prayer, recalling God's former deeds.
Psa.143.structure: Hear my prayer, my spirit faints, I remember the days of old, teach me your way, lead me on level ground.
Psa.143.world_behind: The psalm's posture of hands toward the sanctuary and defeat is that of a worshipper who cannot yet reach it.

deep_background.note: Mountain tracks were uneven and dangerous, so a straight path is a prayer for safety and direction in one image.

Psa.144.occasion: A royal prayer for deliverance and prosperity.
Psa.144.structure: Blessed be my rock, man's days like a shadow, part the heavens, rescue me from foreign hands, a new song, the blessed state described.
Psa.144.world_behind: Kings led armies and relied on city walls and storehouses, so a prayer for sons like cornerstones was a prayer for future defence.

deep_background.note: Diplomatic oaths were routinely broken, so the psalm's request for deliverance from strange lips is about treaty betrayal.

Psa.145.occasion: A praise psalm in acrostic form, the last Davidic psalm.
Psa.145.structure: I will extol you, generation to generation, the LORD is gracious and merciful, near to all who call, he upholds the falling, he is near to all who call.
Psa.145.world_behind: Acrostic praise was a teaching form, and its completeness announced that no letter, and so no part of life, is left out of praise.

deep_background.note: God's kingship is described as ever enduring, a political claim in a world where dynasties rose and fell quickly.

Psa.146.occasion: The first of five closing Hallelujah psalms.
Psa.146.structure: Praise the LORD, put no trust in princes, the LORD made heaven and earth, he executes justice for the oppressed, he lifts up the bowed down.
Psa.146.world_behind: Court poets praised kings and their power, and this psalm refuses that practice by transferring unreserved trust to God alone.

deep_background.note: Ancient Hebrew thought tied life to breath, so the mortality stated here is total, not merely political.

Psa.147.occasion: A praise psalm for the restoration of Jerusalem.
Psa.147.structure: Praise the LORD, he builds Jerusalem and gathers the outcasts, he heals the brokenhearted, he counts and names the stars, he satisfies the earth with rain.
Psa.147.world_behind: Rebuilding walls and streets after exile was communal labour, so the psalm's claim is political as well as spiritual.

deep_background.concept: He gives the beasts their food
deep_background.note: The psalm's attention to animals signalled a creator who cares for all life, an argument against thinking only of the nation.

Psa.148.structure: Praise from the heavens, angels, sun and moon, then from the earth, creatures and kings, then the horn of the people.
Psa.148.world_behind: The psalm structures creation in a hierarchy of praise, the same way an ancient court assembled its servants.

deep_background.note: The horn is both the appeal for strength and the animal horn used for alarm, so the closing line gathers both.

Psa.149.occasion: A praise psalm for the congregation in Zion.
Psa.149.structure: Sing a new song, let the children of Zion be glad, the LORD takes pleasure in his people, let the saints execute judgment with a two-edged sword.
Psa.149.world_behind: Two-edged swords were advanced weapons, used both to pierce and cut, so the psalm's martial imagery is deliberately foreign to most of the book.

deep_background.note: Sleeping on watch or in danger, the faithful sang, a practice reflected in later monastic worship.

Psa.150.occasion: The closing doxology of the whole psalter.
Psa.150.structure: Praise him in the sanctuary, praise him for his mighty deeds, praise with trumpet, lute, harp, timbrel, strings, pipe and cymbals, let everything that has breath praise the LORD.
Psa.150.world_behind: The list of instruments is the temple orchestra, each one part of the daily and festal worship cycle.

deep_background.note: The final word is based on the divine name, turning a closing doxology into a play on God's own title.

Psa.42.occasion: A lament of one cut off from the sanctuary, the first of Book II.
Psa.42.structure: As a deer pants for water, tears day and night, remembering the festal crowd, a refrain of hope, the deep calling to deep.
Psa.42.world_behind: The psalmist is taunted by neighbours and cannot join the pilgrimage, a social as well as spiritual exile.

deep_background.note: Waterfalls and underground springs north of Israel, at the sources of the Jordan, produced the roar the image depends on.

Psa.43.occasion: A continuation of Psalm 42, pleading for vindication.
Psa.43.structure: Vindicate me O God, why have you cast me off, send out your light and truth, then I will go to the altar of God with joy.
Psa.43.world_behind: Going to the altar required a clean standing and a public procession, which the psalmist is currently denied.

deep_background.note: The pair function as guides through hostile country, the way a royal envoy travelled under a safe-conduct.

Psa.44.occasion: A national lament after a defeat, rehearsing past deliverance.
Psa.44.structure: We have heard with our ears, God drove out the nations, but now you have rejected us, we are counted as sheep for slaughter, a final appeal to rise and help.
Psa.44.world_behind: Defeat meant loss of land, tribute and status, and nations read such loss as evidence that their god had failed.

deep_background.note: The image of covenant people as sacrificial animals is the one Paul quotes in Romans on suffering and hope.

Psa.45.occasion: A royal wedding song for a king's marriage.
Psa.45.structure: Prologue to an excellent theme, the king's beauty and victory, weapons blessed, the queen's arrival from a foreign land, the bride's new loyalty, an everlasting name.
Psa.45.world_behind: Royal marriages sealed alliances, and the bride's departure from her family is reflected in the advice to forget her people.

deep_background.note: Ophir was the legendary source of the finest gold, used to describe maximum royal wealth.

Psa.46.occasion: A Zion hymn of confidence in God's presence, a refuge in upheaval.
Psa.46.structure: God is our refuge, therefore we will not fear, the city of God is glad, the nations rage, be still and know, the LORD of hosts is with us.
Psa.46.world_behind: Jerusalem's defence was its water supply and walls; the psalm's river imagery reverses the siege anxiety of a walled city.

deep_background.note: The command is addressed to the raging nations, not to the worshipper's heart, and means cease fighting.

Psa.47.occasion: A psalm celebrating God's kingship over the nations.
Psa.47.structure: Clap your hands all peoples, God is the great king, he subdues peoples, God ascends with a shout, sing praises with understanding.
Psa.47.world_behind: The ark's ascent to Zion was re-enacted in procession with trumpet and shout, which the psalm's movement of praise relies on.

deep_background.note: Shields belonged to kings and their gods; calling them God's means every defence ultimately belongs to him.

Psa.48.occasion: A Zion hymn praising the city's security.
Psa.48.structure: Great is the LORD in the city of our God, beautiful in elevation, kings assembled and fled, God establishes it forever, we have thought on your steadfast love.
Psa.48.world_behind: Ancient cities were praised by listing their walls, gates and towers, and the psalm uses that same civic rhetoric.

deep_background.note: Long-distance trading ships became proverbial for wealth and power, so their breaking signals the collapse of imperial commerce.

Psa.49.occasion: A wisdom psalm on the futility of wealth.
Psa.49.structure: Call to all peoples, why fear the rich, no one can ransom a brother, the fate of the foolish, the upright will have dominion, do not fear when men grow rich.
Psa.49.world_behind: Ransom in Israel was the price paid to release a life, and the psalm's claim is that no such price exists for death.

deep_background.note: The psalm pictures death as a shepherd driving the wealthy into the grave, reversing the pastoral image of God.

Psa.50.occasion: A covenant lawsuit psalm in which God speaks.
Psa.50.structure: The LORD summons the earth, he judges his people, he rejects empty sacrifice, he calls for thanksgiving and vows, he rebukes the wicked who quote his law.
Psa.50.world_behind: The prophetic lawsuit form was used at the temple, where the accuser and the accused were both ritual participants.

deep_background.concept: The cattle on a thousand hills
deep_background.note: Because God owns every animal, sacrifice cannot be feeding him, so the psalm attacks sacrifice as payment rather than trust.

Pro.1.occasion: The book's prologue: why the proverbs exist and who they are for.
Pro.1.structure: Purpose statement, the motto 'the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge', a father's warning against violent gain, and wisdom crying in the public square while fools refuse her.
Pro.1.world_behind: Instruction of this kind belonged to the household and the court school. A father teaching a son was the ordinary channel of education in Israel, and the street preaching of wisdom is presented as a woman calling where commerce and courts met.

deep_background.note: Not terror but the settled posture of taking God seriously; the phrase anchors the whole book.

Pro.2.occasion: A father urges his son to pursue wisdom as men pursue ore.
Pro.2.structure: Conditional appeals to receive and search, then the promise that wisdom comes from the LORD, then her protective work: saving from crooked men and from the forbidden woman.
Pro.2.world_behind: Mining and smelting were known crafts, so silver and hidden treasure were natural images of costly pursuit. The adulteress is a recurring danger in the book, addressed to young men entering adult life.

deep_background.note: Ancient prospecting was slow and deliberate, an image of patience rather than sudden insight.

Pro.3.occasion: Wisdom as a way of living trustingly and generously.
Pro.3.structure: Keep steadfast love and faithfulness, trust the LORD with all your heart, honour him with firstfruits, accept discipline, then a poem on wisdom's worth and a call to neighbour love.
Pro.3.world_behind: Firstfruits assumed an agricultural economy where the opening of the harvest belonged to God before the household ate. Discipline language reflects a father's correction of a son.

deep_background.note: Giving the first and best was a public declaration that the land and its yield were not ultimately the family's own.

Pro.4.occasion: A father passes on what his own father taught him.
Pro.4.structure: Three generations of instruction, wisdom as the principal thing to acquire, the two paths of light and darkness, and a closing charge to guard the heart, mouth, eyes and feet.
Pro.4.world_behind: The path metaphor came from a world of foot travel where the route chosen was visible and irreversible. Heart meant the settled centre of thought and will, not sentiment alone.

deep_background.note: Israelite wisdom consistently frames ethics as a road: you are always on one of two, never off both.

Pro.5.occasion: A father's blunt warning against sexual sin.
Pro.5.structure: The seductress's speech sweet as honey, her end bitter as wormwood, a charge to enjoy one's own wife, and a warning that a man's ways are before the LORD.
Pro.5.world_behind: Marriage in Israel was the household's foundation, and adultery threatened inheritance, reputation and community standing. Water and cistern imagery describes marital intimacy as one's own source.

deep_background.note: A bitter desert plant used as the standard image for something that turns sweet to poison.

Pro.6.occasion: Practical warnings against folly in daily dealings.
Pro.6.structure: Surety for a stranger, the sluggard and the ant, the worthless man, seven things God hates, and a repeat of the adultery warning with its cost measured.
Pro.6.world_behind: Standing surety meant pledging your own goods for another man's debt in a village economy with no banks. The ant was a standard example of instinctive industry in the ancient Near East.

deep_background.note: The numbered list is a teaching device, fixing sins in memory for a culture that learned by recitation.

Pro.7.occasion: A vivid narrative warning about seduction.
Pro.7.structure: Charge to keep instruction as the pupil of the eye, then a scene: dusk, a young man without sense, a smooth-tongued woman with a prepared bed and an absent husband, and his ruin pictured as an ox to the slaughter.
Pro.7.world_behind: The scene is set at evening when the streets emptied and lamps were lit. An altar of peace offerings supplied the meat for her feast, giving the invitation a religious colouring that made it harder to refuse.

deep_background.note: The most sensitive and protected part of the body, used as the image for guarding teaching against any intrusion.

Pro.8.occasion: Wisdom speaks in her own voice as a public teacher.
Pro.8.structure: Wisdom calls at the gates and crossroads, claims to speak truth and hate pride, then describes being present at creation as a master craftsman delighting before God, and closes by promising life to those who find her.
Pro.8.world_behind: City gates were courts, markets and meeting places, so wisdom's pulpit is the busiest public space rather than a shrine. Craftsmanship imagery reflects a world that built by hand and valued the skilled artisan.

deep_background.note: The passage is poetic personification, not a claim that wisdom is a second deity; it grounds moral order in the way the world was made.

Pro.9.occasion: Two invitations, two houses, two ends.
Pro.9.structure: Wisdom builds her house, mixes wine and sends her servants to call the simple to her table; then Folly sits at her door with stolen water and bread eaten in secret; the chapter ends on the root of the matter, the fear of the LORD.
Pro.9.world_behind: A house with seven pillars was an image of a complete and well-built dwelling. Banquet invitation and wine mixing were signs of deliberate hospitality, contrasting with folly's secret and stolen food.

deep_background.note: The proverb names the real pull of sin: not the object but the secrecy and the sense of acquisition.

Pro.10.occasion: The first of Solomon's collected couplets.
Pro.10.structure: Short two-line contrasts, mostly righteous against wicked: wealth and poverty, the tongue, love that covers offenses, diligence against slackness, and the expectation of the upright being granted.
Pro.10.world_behind: Proverbs of this shape were memorised in households. In an agrarian village, diligence meant harvest security and laziness meant hunger, so the moral claim rested on visible economics.

deep_background.note: The second line sharpens the first by contrast, the basic engine of Hebrew poetic teaching.

Pro.11.occasion: Honesty in trade and its social consequences.
Pro.11.structure: False scales, pride before a fall, wealth that fails in the day of wrath, generosity that prospers, the righteous who deliver a city, and the tree of life versus the one who wins souls.
Pro.11.world_behind: Scales and weights were the ordinary point of contact between buyer and seller, and dishonest ones were a common fraud. The city saved by upright men reflects small walled towns where a few good households could change the whole community's fate.

deep_background.note: Ancient weights were stones carried in a bag; tampering was easy and hard to prove, which is why the law addresses it so often.

Pro.12.occasion: The disciplined life against the self-satisfied one.
Pro.12.structure: Love of instruction, a good wife as a crown, the words of the wicked as ambush, the diligent hand ruling, anxiety weighing the heart down, and a cheerful word doing good like medicine.
Pro.12.world_behind: Agriculture and animal care frame the images, from the sluggard who will not roast his catch to the path of the righteous shining brighter. Family reputation rested heavily on the wife's management of the household.

deep_background.note: Speech is treated as a physical force in this book, doing real damage or real repair.

Pro.13.occasion: The tongue, wealth and correction in the household.
Pro.13.structure: A wise son hears instruction, the fruit of the mouth, wealth gained hastily, hope deferred making the heart sick, and the rod of correction paired with love.
Pro.13.world_behind: Corporal correction of a child was normal in the ancient household and is framed here as love rather than severity. Wealth 'gained hastily' refers to speculation and windfall rather than steady trade.

deep_background.note: One of the book's few windows into inner emotional life, naming the sickness of long waiting.

Pro.14.occasion: Wisdom builds a house; folly tears it down with her own hands.
Pro.14.structure: The wise woman and the foolish, the fear of the LORD as a fountain of life, the poor who is hated and the rich who has many friends, a cheerful heart as good medicine, and a nation's righteousness lifting it up.
Pro.14.world_behind: Households were the economic unit, so a wife's competence built the family's standing. Public shame and honour mattered deeply in a small community where reputation was inherited.

deep_background.note: In a dry land, a spring was survival; the image makes wisdom a source rather than a rule.

Pro.15.occasion: The power of a measured answer.
Pro.15.structure: A soft answer turning away wrath, the eyes of the LORD in every place, a merry heart as continual feast, the way of the sluggard as a hedge of thorns, and the fear of the LORD as instruction in wisdom.
Pro.15.world_behind: Hospitality and shared meals were the setting for the 'feast' image. Thorns hedging a path describe an ordinary hazard of travel, used here for self-inflicted delay.

deep_background.note: The proverb assumes anger is a shared social force that one party can deflect by tone alone.

Pro.16.structure: The LORD weighs motives, commit your works to him, pride before destruction, the king's throne established by righteousness, honest scales, and the casting of the lot into the lap.
Pro.16.world_behind: The lot was a real decision-making tool in Israel, used for allocating land and identifying guilt. The king is pictured as a judge whose verdicts carried life and death in a society without appeal.

deep_background.note: A lot was cast into a garment's fold and read as divine direction, which is why the proverb places the outcome with God.

Pro.17.occasion: Friendship, family peace and the value of quiet.
Pro.17.structure: Better a dry morsel with quiet than a feast with strife, the LORD tests hearts, a friend loves at all times, a cheerful heart as medicine, and a rebuke that lands better on a wise man than a hundred blows on a fool.
Pro.17.world_behind: Household meals were modest and shared, so the contrast between a dry crust in peace and a house full of feasting with quarrelling would be immediately felt.

deep_background.note: Kinship language applied to friendship shows the strength of chosen bonds in a society organised around family.

Pro.18.occasion: Speech, isolation and the name of the LORD.
Pro.18.structure: The unfriendly man isolates himself, a fool's mouth brings ruin, the name of the LORD is a strong tower, wealth as a walled city, the tongue's power over life and death, and a friend who sticks closer than a brother.
Pro.18.world_behind: Towers and walled cities were literal refuges in a landscape of raids. The gate imagery in this chapter reflects the place where disputes were heard and reputations were made.

deep_background.note: In Hebrew thought a name carries the character of the one who bears it, so calling on the name is calling on the person.

Pro.19.occasion: Poverty, patience and the fear of the LORD.
Pro.19.structure: Better the poor who walks in integrity, wealth adds many friends, a man's discretion makes him slow to anger, a prudent wife is from the LORD, and the one who is kind to the poor lends to the LORD.
Pro.19.world_behind: Bribery and patronage shaped ancient courts, so the proverb that a gift in secret persuades is observation, not endorsement. Poverty was close to slavery for debt, which gives the generosity sayings their edge.

deep_background.note: Mercy to the poor is framed as a loan God himself repays, dignifying the recipient rather than the giver.

Pro.20.structure: Wine as a mocker, the king's wrath as a lion's roar, the sluggard who will not plough, diverse weights as an abomination, and the spirit of man as the lamp of the LORD searching the inward parts.
Pro.20.world_behind: Thresholds and threshing floors appear as everyday settings. Two sets of weights, one for buying and one for selling, was the standard ancient fraud the prophets attacked.

deep_background.note: Cheating in trade was a covenant offense, not merely bad business, because it denied that God sees the marketplace.

Pro.21.occasion: The king's heart in the LORD's hand, and justice that outweighs ritual.
Pro.21.structure: The king's heart as a watercourse, doing justice as more acceptable than sacrifice, the proud lamp of the wicked, the quarrelsome wife, and the horse prepared for battle but the victory belonging to the LORD.
Pro.21.world_behind: Watercourses were irrigation channels a farmer could turn by hand, the image behind God directing a king. Sacrifice without justice was a live prophetic complaint in Israel, so the proverb joins that argument.
