deep_background.note: The same claim is made by Amos and Isaiah, showing wisdom and prophecy sharing a moral core.

Pro.22.occasion: A good name, the training of a child, and the words of the wise.
Pro.22.structure: A good name over great riches, train up a child in the way he should go, the rich and poor meet together before God, the borrower as servant to the lender, and an appendix of sayings of the wise on boundaries and integrity.
Pro.22.world_behind: Debt slavery was real, so the borrower's servitude was a social fact, not a metaphor. A 'good name' meant a family's standing in a village where it could not be escaped.

deep_background.note: The verb carries the sense of initiating, tied to the child's own disposition rather than a single method.

Pro.23.occasion: Self-control at the table and in appetite.
Pro.23.structure: Do not crave a ruler's delicacies, do not toil for riches that sprout wings, do not move ancient boundary stones, discipline your son, and a closing portrait of wine as a serpent that bites.
Pro.23.world_behind: Banquets with a ruler were political occasions where appetite signalled character. Wine was drunk diluted and mixed, and public drunkenness was a mark of the fool in Israelite wisdom.

deep_background.note: Wealth is pictured as a bird, not as a possession; the image undercuts any sense of security.

Pro.24.occasion: Do not envy the wicked; wisdom builds a house.
Pro.24.structure: Do not envy evil men, a house is built by wisdom, rescue those being led to death, do not gloat at a fallen enemy, the field of the sluggard overgrown with thorns, and a short appendix of further wise sayings.
Pro.24.world_behind: The overgrown field with a broken wall was a familiar sight in an agricultural society where neglect was visible within a season. Gleaning rights and boundary markers governed rural life.

deep_background.note: The claim that ignorance is no excuse for inaction is one of the book's sharpest moral statements.

Pro.25.occasion: Sayings copied by the men of Hezekiah, Judah's reforming king.
Pro.25.structure: The glory of God in concealment and kings in searching things out, remove the wicked from the king's presence, do not exalt yourself at the table, a word fitly spoken as apples of gold, and coals heaped on an enemy's head.
Pro.25.world_behind: This collection is explicitly royal: copying and editing proverbs was court work under a reforming king. Apples of gold in silver settings describe actual decorative metalwork in which fruit motifs were set in silver.

deep_background.note: The heading shows the book was compiled over centuries, not dictated in one sitting.

Pro.26.occasion: The fool, the sluggard and the troublemaker.
Pro.26.structure: Honour is unfitting for a fool, answer a fool according to his folly, the sluggard who will not go out for fear of a lion, the whisperer who separates friends, and the mouth that seems earnest but conceals malice.
Pro.26.world_behind: Lions still roamed the region, and the sluggard's excuse is a comic exaggeration of a real danger. Whispering in a village meant spreading a report nobody could trace to its source.

deep_background.note: Two consecutive proverbs give opposite advice, teaching that the wise must judge when speech helps and when it feeds folly.

Pro.27.occasion: Friendship, reputation and knowing your flock.
Pro.27.structure: Do not boast of tomorrow, let another praise you, the wounds of a friend are faithful, iron sharpens iron, know well the state of your flocks, and the face answered in water.
Pro.27.world_behind: Herd and flock imagery reflects a mixed pastoral economy. Public praise mattered because honour was the currency of standing, and self-praise was considered a social offence.

deep_background.note: Correction from a friend is classed with healing, against flattery, which is classed with kissing an enemy.

Pro.28.occasion: The wicked flee; the righteous are bold.
Pro.28.structure: The guilty conscience runs when no one pursues, a poor man who oppresses the poor, those who forsake the law praising the wicked, the one who confesses and forsakes finding mercy, and the man who trusts in his own heart as a fool.
Pro.28.world_behind: Justice was administered at the gate by elders, so a corrupt ruler distorted the only court most people would ever see. Confession and restitution were legal acts as well as religious ones.

deep_background.note: The lion was the emblem of fearless strength in Israel and Judah, used here for a clear conscience.

Pro.29.occasion: Discipline, rulers and the fear of man.
Pro.29.structure: A man who hardens his neck, when the righteous rule the people rejoice, the rod and reproof giving wisdom, the fear of man as a snare, and the LORD giving strength to his people.
Pro.29.world_behind: Hardening the neck is a farming image of a stubborn ox refusing the yoke. The joy of the people under a righteous ruler assumes kingship as the ordinary structure of national life.

deep_background.note: The snare image says that pleasing people traps you, and the alternative given is trust in the LORD.

Pro.30.occasion: The words of Agur, a teacher outside the main collection.
Pro.30.structure: A confession of ignorance before God, a request for neither poverty nor riches but daily bread, warnings against slandering a servant, the leech's daughters, and a series of numerical sayings about small things that are wise.
Pro.30.world_behind: Agur is otherwise unknown, evidence that Israel's wisdom drew on teachers beyond the royal court. The prayer for a middle portion reflects a society where both extremes, riches and debt, were spiritually dangerous.

deep_background.note: One of the few explicit prayers in Proverbs, asking for sufficiency rather than success.

Pro.31.occasion: The words of King Lemuel's mother, closing with the woman of valour.
Pro.31.structure: A mother's charge about wine, women and justice for the poor, then an acrostic poem describing a capable wife who trades, manages a household, gives to the poor, and is praised in the gates.
Pro.31.world_behind: The poem's woman runs a household economy: buying linen, planting a vineyard, trading with merchants, and hiring servants. That is an accurate picture of a wealthy ancient household where the wife directed domestic production.

deep_background.note: The same Hebrew phrase describes a warrior; the poem applies military strength language to household competence.

Ecc.1.occasion: The Preacher opens with the verdict that everything is vapour.
Ecc.1.structure: The motto 'vanity of vanities', the endless cycles of generations, sun, wind and rivers, the claim that nothing is new, and the weariness of seeing with no gain.
Ecc.1.world_behind: The speaker is a wisdom teacher who has observed life systematically. The cyclical view of nature stands against the linear hope of the prophets, making this book an argument inside Israel's own tradition.

deep_background.note: The Hebrew word means vapour or breath, not worthlessness: fleeting, ungraspable, impossible to hold.

Ecc.2.occasion: A test of pleasure, building and toil as sources of meaning.
Ecc.2.structure: Wine, houses, gardens and singers are accumulated, then the verdict that all is vapour, then the observation that wisdom exceeds folly but both end in death, and the first call to enjoy one's food and work as God's gift.
Ecc.2.world_behind: The list of projects mirrors what an ancient king could actually commission: vineyards, parks, reservoirs, singers, slaves. Enjoyment of food and labour is framed as a gift received rather than a right seized.

deep_background.note: The idea that God assigns each person a share runs through the book and keeps pleasure from becoming accumulation.

Ecc.3.occasion: A time for everything, and eternity set in the human heart.
Ecc.3.structure: The poem of fourteen pairs of times, the claim that God made everything fitting in its time, the limits of human comprehension, and the conclusion that there is nothing better than to rejoice and do good.
Ecc.3.world_behind: The poem maps the ordinary events of an agrarian life, from planting to mourning, and assumes a world where what happens is largely outside individual control.

deep_background.note: The phrase explains why humans long for pattern in a life they cannot see the end of.

Ecc.4.occasion: Oppression, rivalry and the value of a companion.
Ecc.4.structure: Tears of the oppressed with no comforter, toil driven by envy, the two hands full of quiet, and the threefold cord that is not quickly broken.
Ecc.4.world_behind: The book speaks from a society with courts, patronage and debt, where the powerless had no advocate. The cord image comes from rope made of twisted strands.

deep_background.note: Companionship is offered as the one reliable hedge against a life that cannot be controlled.

Ecc.5.occasion: Rash vows and the trap of wealth.
Ecc.5.structure: Guard your steps at God's house, let your words be few, do not delay a vow, the love of money never satisfied, the labourer's sweet sleep, and the ending that it is good to eat and toil in one's few days.
Ecc.5.world_behind: Vows were binding and enforced at the sanctuary, so the warning addresses a real practice of bargaining with God. The sleeping labourer versus the sleepless rich man is a picture of a simple economy.

deep_background.note: The instruction reflects a temple setting where speech was costly and silence was reverence.

Ecc.6.structure: A man given wealth, honour and children who cannot enjoy any of it, the stillborn who finds more rest, and the closing claim that all the labour of man is for his mouth and yet the appetite is not filled.
Ecc.6.world_behind: Children and long life were the standard markers of blessing in Israel, so the picture of a man with both but no enjoyment deliberately overturns the expected reward.

deep_background.note: The book's repeated refrain: the difference between having and receiving is God's giving.

Ecc.7.occasion: Wisdom in the face of grief and the limits of righteousness.
Ecc.7.structure: Better a good name than ointment, the house of mourning over the house of feasting, patience over pride, the man who fears God, and the closing admission that no one is righteous and wisdom remains beyond reach.
Ecc.7.world_behind: Mourning and feasting were the two defining social gatherings of an ancient village, and visiting the house of mourning was a duty. Ointment was expensive and used on festive occasions.

deep_background.note: The claim that death teaches better than celebration is the book's argument in miniature.

Ecc.8.occasion: Authority, injustice and the limits of human justice.
Ecc.8.structure: Keep the king's command, the wise man's face and his knowledge of times, the wicked buried with honour, the delay of judgment, and the call to enjoy life because no one knows the work of God.
Ecc.8.world_behind: Kingship meant personal command and personal danger for those who crossed it. Burials with honour were public verdicts on a life, which sharpens the complaint about wicked men receiving them.

deep_background.note: The observation that sentence against evil work is not executed speedily explains why the heart of men is set on evil.

Ecc.9.occasion: One fate for all, and the call to live fully now.
Ecc.9.structure: The righteous and the wicked share the same end, bread eaten with joy and a wife loved in the days of vanity, the race not to the swift, and wisdom that saves a city though no one remembers the poor man who gave it.
Ecc.9.world_behind: Marriage, bread and wine were the ordinary textures of life, and the book anchors its ethics in them rather than in hope of reward after death.

deep_background.note: The phrase marks the book's frame of observation: what can be seen from within this life alone.

Ecc.10.occasion: Folly in high places and small things that spoil much.
Ecc.10.structure: A little folly outweighs wisdom and honour, the wise heart at the right hand, the pit and the hole dug for another, the king as a child, the slothful roof that leaks, and money as the answer to a feast.
Ecc.10.world_behind: Roofs were flat and sealed with mud or plaster that needed annual repair, so the leaking roof is a precise image of neglect. Court politics and the danger of cursing the king in private frame the political sayings.

deep_background.note: The book keeps insisting that small failures carry disproportionate cost, especially where reputation is concerned.

Ecc.11.occasion: Risk, generosity and the uncertainty of the future.
Ecc.11.structure: Cast your bread on the waters, give a portion to seven or eight, do not watch the wind and never sow, the light of day as sweet, and the charge to remember the days of darkness are coming.
Ecc.11.world_behind: The charge to give to seven or eight reflects the need for diversified patronage and alms in a world without insurance. Weather watching was the farmer's constant occupation and the proverb forbids it as paralysis.

deep_background.note: Interpreted as either maritime trade or generosity, the point stands either way: act without guaranteeing the return.

Ecc.12.occasion: The book's final word: remember God before the years of decline.
Ecc.12.structure: Poetry on the failing body as a decaying house, the golden bowl and the broken pitcher, the return of dust to earth and spirit to God, the epilogue's verdict that all has been heard and the whole duty is to fear God and keep his commands.
Ecc.12.world_behind: The imagery draws on water systems of a city: keepers of the house, grinders at the mill, windows growing dark, and a cistern's wheel breaking at a well.

deep_background.note: The one imperative the book lands on, offered before the body can no longer carry it out.

Sng.1.occasion: The opening exchange of longing between the woman and the man.
Sng.1.structure: Desire for his kisses, the daughters of Jerusalem as a chorus, the woman's self-description as dark yet lovely, and an invitation to the pastures where he shepherds.
Sng.1.world_behind: The poem belongs to the world of vineyards, shepherds and royal halls. Dark skin marks outdoor labour rather than ethnicity, and the daughters of Jerusalem serve as the observing chorus in a culture where young women spoke together.

deep_background.note: The poem is written as performed speech, with parts that shift between the lovers and the watching women.

Sng.2.occasion: Springtime and the invitation to come away.
Sng.2.structure: The woman as a lily among thorns, the man as an apple tree in the forest, the season of singing and the blossoming vines, and the charge not to awaken love until it pleases.
Sng.2.world_behind: The imagery is drawn from the Levantine spring, when rain ends and wildflowers appear. Vineyards in bud and doves in the rocks fix the poem to a specific landscape and season.

deep_background.note: A refrain repeated three times, guarding against forcing desire before its time.

Sng.3.occasion: A night search through the city, then a wedding procession.
Sng.3.structure: The woman searches the streets at night for her beloved, finds him and holds him, then a description of Solomon's wedding procession with its guards and litter.
Sng.3.world_behind: City streets at night were watched by guards, and searching alone was both dangerous and transgressive, which gives the scene its urgency. The processional litter with sixty warriors reflects royal display.

deep_background.note: The watchmen recur later in the poem, becoming figures of obstruction rather than help.

Sng.4.occasion: The man's praise of the woman's beauty, and the garden invitation.
Sng.4.structure: A head-to-foot description using landscape and architecture, the call to come from Lebanon, and the image of the bride as a locked garden and a sealed spring.
Sng.4.world_behind: The comparisons come from trade and architecture: ivory towers, pomegranate orchards, spice beds, and the sealed well that supplied a household. Spices such as myrrh and frankincense were imports of real value.

deep_background.note: An enclosed garden was both a sign of wealth and an image of privacy and exclusivity.

Sng.5.occasion: Absence after the wedding night, and another night search.
Sng.5.structure: The man knocks, the woman delays, he is gone, she searches the streets, the watchmen strike her, and she describes his beauty to the women of Jerusalem.
Sng.5.world_behind: Doors, bolts and street patrols shape the scene. The description of the beloved as ruddy and outstanding among ten thousand uses the language of precious metal and polished stone.

deep_background.note: The delay is a real human moment, not a moral failure, and the poem treats lounging longing without condemnation.

Sng.6.occasion: The woman is sought and praised, and the garden is revisited.
Sng.6.structure: Where has the beloved gone, the woman's confident answer, the man's praise as unique among many, and the return to the garden imagery of nuts and vines.
Sng.6.world_behind: The comparison to a city and an army with banners draws on the martial imagery familiar in the period, applied here as praise rather than threat.

deep_background.note: The names used between the lovers are affectionate titles rather than descriptions.

Sng.7.occasion: Praise of the woman's beauty, and her invitation.
Sng.7.structure: A dance described in images of royalty, a body praised with landscape and craftsmanship, then her invitation to the fields and vineyards where she will give her love.
Sng.7.world_behind: The poem references wine, wheat, ivory and purple, all markers of a prosperous household. Vineyard and field imagery keeps returning love to the ordinary work of the season.

deep_background.note: The woman takes the initiative in inviting, which is a notable feature of the whole poem.

Sng.8.occasion: The closing poem: love as strong as death.
Sng.8.structure: A wish for public recognition of the relationship, the seal on the heart, love strong as death with its flashes of fire, the value of the vineyard, and a final refrain about not awakening love.
Sng.8.world_behind: A seal was a personal mark of ownership and identity, worn on the hand or hung on a cord, making the seal on the heart an image of inseparable belonging.

deep_background.note: The poem ends by comparing love to the one force no one resists, and calling its flame unquenchable.

Isa.1.occasion: Isaiah's opening indictment of Judah's rebellion and hollow worship.
Isa.1.structure: A lawsuit speech: the LORD accuses, the people's sacrifices are rejected, a call to wash and obey, then Zion refined by judgment.
Isa.1.world_behind: Assyria is rising and Judah is secure but corrupt; prophets brought covenant lawsuits against the nation in the form of a legal dispute.

deep_background.note: Calling Judah's rulers 'Sodom' invokes Genesis 19 to say the nation's moral state matches a city already judged.

Isa.2.occasion: The mountain of the LORD and the day of pride humbled.
Isa.2.structure: Zion exalted and nations streaming up, then a reversal into the day of the LORD against human pride, ending with a call to stop trusting in man.
Isa.2.world_behind: Jerusalem sat on a hill with the temple as its crown, so 'mountain of the LORD' meant the city itself as the place of God's presence.

deep_background.note: Iron plow tips and pruning hooks were ordinary farm tools, so the image means an economy converted from war to food.

Isa.3.occasion: Anarchy in Judah and judgment on its leaders and wealthy women.
Isa.3.structure: Leadership removed, incompetence promoted, the LORD enters judgment, then a oracle against the finery of Jerusalem's daughters.
Isa.3.world_behind: Elders and princes governed at the city gate; losing them meant losing courts, defense, and food distribution at once.

deep_background.note: Justice and commerce happened in the city gate, so the removal of elders collapses the whole civic order.

Isa.4.occasion: The branch of the LORD and purged Zion after judgment.
Isa.4.structure: A brief transitional oracle: the survivors are cleansed by a spirit of judgment, then the branch of the LORD becomes beauty for the remnant under a canopy of cloud and fire.
Isa.4.world_behind: The cloud and fire recall the wilderness tabernacle, presented here as returning to shelter a restored city.

deep_background.note: Hebrew tsemach means a sprout from a cut stump, the same image later used for the Davidic heir.

Isa.29.occasion: Ariel besieged, then delivered, and a warning about lip-service.
Isa.29.structure: Jerusalem humbled but defended, then judgment on those whose hearts are far away, ending with the deaf hearing and the potter's clay.
Isa.29.world_behind: Ariel means lion of God, a name for Zion suggesting strength; the besieging armies camp against it.

deep_background.note: Potters worked clay on a wheel in every village, so the image of maker and made was concrete, not abstract.

Isa.30.occasion: Egypt relied on and found worthless; grace in the late groove, but grace comes.
Isa.30.structure: Woe to those carrying treasure to Egypt, the collapse of that hope, a fireside oracle of grace (actually a few words in a corner), and God's voice behind them.
Isa.30.world_behind: Judah paid tribute for Egyptian cavalry, the most practical military hope against Assyria.

deep_background.note: A pledge recorded in a document and sealed was proof a matter was settled, the image of a fixed fate.

Isa.31.occasion: Woe to those trusting in chariots, but the LORD defends Zion.
Isa.31.structure: Woe to those going down to Egypt, the LORD descends like a lion, and Jerusalem is protected like a bird.
Isa.31.world_behind: Egypt supplied horses and chariots in bulk, the cutting-edge military technology of the day.

deep_background.note: Horses cost more than cattle, so chariots signified national wealth and alliance, not just speed.

Isa.32.occasion: A righteous king and the Spirit poured out.
Isa.32.structure: A king reigns as a shelter, then a desolate city lament, then the Spirit outpoured, turning desert to field and masons worked fields.
Isa.32.world_behind: Grain and vineyards grew in the hill country; a city bereft its fields lay abandoned.

deep_background.note: Grain fields and vineyards were the two pillars of hill country farming, so restoring them restores ordinary life.

Isa.33.occasion: Woe to the destroyer and the King in beauty.
Isa.33.structure: The destroyer promised the same, a night of terror, the nations scattered, and the righteous Zion described as a place of rivers and none of the king's splendor.
Isa.33.world_behind: Jerusalem depended on water held in cisterns and a spring, so a city with rivers meant a poem of safety, not geology.

deep_background.note: Tent pegs held up the whole shelter, so stakes that are never pulled means security nobody can dismantle.

Isa.34.occasion: Judgment on Edom, the book of the LORD.
Isa.34.structure: Nations assembled for slaughter, Edom a smoking desert, then a public reading call to the book so nothing in it fails.
Isa.34.world_behind: Edom held the sandstone highlands south of the Dead Sea, its fall a full bordered picture of judgment.

deep_background.note: Unclean scavengers inhabit the destroyed land, so the sign of judgment is a human absence, not a human city.

Isa.35.occasion: The desert blossoms and the ransomed return.
Isa.35.structure: The wilderness blooms, weak hands are strengthened, blind eyes open, and a highway of holiness brings the redeemed home singing.
Isa.35.world_behind: The road from Babylon to Judah cut harsh steppe, a place travelers feared.

deep_background.note: Kings built highways for armies and merchants, so a road in the wilderness images royal care for returning exiles.

Isa.36.structure: A field commander at the aqueduct mocks Hezekiah and the LORD, and the king's officials answer in mourning.
Isa.36.world_behind: The siege was announced at the point where a city loses its water; Sennacherib had destroyed the cisterns.

deep_background.note: The laundry field outside the wall carried water, so that is where the enemy's demand is delivered.

Isa.37.structure: Hezekiah spreads the letter in the temple, Isaiah gives the oracle, and the angel strikes 185,000, with Sennacherib killed at home.
Isa.37.world_behind: An Assyrian king's bodyguards often included sons predictably ambitious; the murder by his sons fits the record pattern.

deep_background.note: The prayer reaches the one enthroned between the cherubim, so the ark image is the appeal to real rule.

Isa.38.structure: The prophet announces death, Hezekiah prays and weeps, the sign of the sundial marks fifteen added years, and the king writes a psalm.
Isa.38.world_behind: The illness is a skin outbreak treated with a fig poultice, an ordinary household remedy of the period.

deep_background.note: The shadow on Ahaz's stairway gave the king a measurable sign he could check himself, not a private feeling.

Isa.39.occasion: Babylonian envoys and the prediction of exile.
Isa.39.structure: Envoys from Babylon see the royal treasure, Isaiah asks what they saw, and exile in Babylon is announced.
Isa.39.world_behind: Babylon was still a subject state under Assyria, so this envoy was a political probe dressed as a courtesy visit.

deep_background.note: Showing the storehouse flaunts wealth and, more importantly, tells the future enemy exactly what the city has.

Isa.40.occasion: Comfort for a people, and an incomparable God.
Isa.40.structure: A voice in the wilderness prepares a road, the word of God stands forever, then the LORD as shepherd beyond counsel, ending with eagles.
Isa.40.world_behind: Kings had highways prepared ahead of them; a road in the desert was a royal project, in the wilderness?

deep_background.note: Vultures and eagles ride thermals without labor, an image used in kingship inscriptions too.

Isa.41.occasion: Israel summoned and idols found worthless.
Isa.41.structure: Coastlands summoned to court, the servant taken by the hand, then a satire where the idol is bolted down and cannot move.
Isa.41.world_behind: An idol backed with nails was a standard statue-making technique, so the picture is technical, not comic.

deep_background.note: Idols were fixed in a shrine so they would not tip, which the prophet reads as a confession of powerlessness.

Isa.42.occasion: The Servant song and a new song.
Isa.42.structure: The Servant brings justice quietly to the nations, the LORD sings a new song, then Israel is named blind and deaf servant.
Isa.42.world_behind: Nations are summoned as witnesses in a courtroom scene, and the Servant is presented as the evidence of God's justice.

deep_background.note: A linen wick gone black but not broken, the picture of faint hope the Servant refuses to snuff out.

Isa.43.occasion: Redemption announced, rivers in the desert.
Isa.43.structure: Do not fear, for I have redeemed you, the exodus pattern repeated, then the blind witness called to testify.
Isa.43.world_behind: Ransoms and prices were legal terms of the slave and temple markets.

deep_background.note: Water from rock is the wilderness memory, so the promise reads as a second exodus.

Isa.44.occasion: The Spirit of life poured on the seed, and idols exposed.
Isa.44.structure: A promise of children and the Spirit, then a long satire of the craftsman who makes a god from the same wood he burns.
Isa.44.world_behind: The craftsman selects timber, burns half of it for cooking, and carves the remainder into a god.

deep_background.note: Cyrus is named roughly a century and a half before his rise, and the text treats that as proof of foreknowledge.

Isa.45.occasion: Cyrus anointed and the LORD as only God.
Isa.45.structure: The LORD gives Cyrus victory and doors, then turns to say he alone is God to all the nations.
Isa.45.world_behind: Anointing was normally for kings chosen by the temple, so the same language applied to a foreign king is deliberately startling.

deep_background.note: Cyrus took wealth from Croesus and opened shrine gates, matching the text's picture of gates opened.

Isa.46.occasion: God carries his own people, but idols need carrying.
Isa.46.structure: Bel and Nebo bow, carried away; the same rock, then the contrast between bearing and being borne.
Isa.46.world_behind: The New Year festival in Babylon paraded Marduk, so the prophet mocks the street theater.

deep_background.note: Bel is Marduk of Babylon and Nebo his son, the two chief gods of the empire, named to be toppled especially far.

Isa.47.structure: A dirge to the virgin city, her occult work exposed, scholarship and stargazing shown to be useless, and her end without remedy.
Isa.47.world_behind: Babylon was famed for astronomy and astrologers, and merchants turned it into a market city serving those needs.

deep_background.note: A daughter means the city personified, treated as a woman whose pride and then dishonor mark her fall.

Isa.48.occasion: Stubborn Israel refined and told to leave.
Isa.48.structure: A charge of hidden obstinacy, the furnace of adversity, then the sudden command to leave Babylon with joy.
Isa.48.world_behind: Furnaces refined gold and silver; the metaphor is that the nation was kept but the next piece came out clean.

deep_background.note: Egypt's iron claw is the earlier furnace, so the exile reads as a second forging, a second refinement.

Isa.49.occasion: The Servant a light to the nations.
Isa.49.structure: The Servant speaks of his calling from the womb, despairs then is honoured, and is given as a covenant to the peoples while Zion is told her children outnumber her ruin.
Isa.49.world_behind: A servant's name inscribed on the palms of the hands echoes the practice of engraving a owner's mark or a memorial on a signet.

deep_background.note: Slaves and seals carried the master's mark, so being written on the hands means permanent, personal claim.

Isa.50.occasion: The Servant's obedience and trust in the dark.
Isa.50.structure: A divorce image denied, the Servant given a taught tongue and an open ear, his back struck, then a challenge to walk in darkness and trust the name.
Isa.50.world_behind: Disciples sat at a teacher's feet and were woken morning by morning, the picture of a learner rather than an orator.

deep_background.note: Pulling the beard was a deliberate public insult in the ancient Near East, not incidental rough handling.

Isa.51.occasion: Look to the rock and the coming salvation.
Isa.51.structure: Israel called to remember Abraham and Sarah, the law goes out as light, the cup of wrath is taken from Jerusalem and handed to her tormentors.
Isa.51.world_behind: Quarrying a nation from one couple is the image of a rock cut for building stone.

deep_background.note: A cup passed around at a banquet, used here for the portion of judgment a city must drink.

Isa.52.occasion: Awake Zion and the messenger's feet.
Isa.52.structure: Jerusalem called to rise, the watchmen sing, and the Servant is introduced as exalted and disfigured.
Isa.52.world_behind: News from a battlefield reached a city only by runner, so beautiful feet means a courier arriving alive.

deep_background.note: Wall guards were the first to see a returning messenger, so their singing marks verified good news.

Isa.53.structure: Who has believed our report, the Servant despised and pierced, the confession that we went astray, then his death, burial, and satisfaction.
Isa.53.world_behind: Healing and sickness are used for both physical and national recovery, and the Servant's grave is assigned with the rich after a criminal's death.

deep_background.note: The onlookers assume suffering proves divine punishment, the assumption the passage then overturns.

Isa.54.occasion: The barren woman sings and the covenant of peace stands.
Isa.54.structure: The childless wife told to enlarge her tent, shame forgotten, the covenant of peace like Noah's oath, and no weapon prospering.
Isa.54.world_behind: Tents were enlarged by adding panels and poles, a real household task for a growing family.

deep_background.note: The promise appeals to an oath already kept once, making this covenant as binding as that one.

Isa.55.structure: Come buy without money, the sure mercies promised to David, seek the LORD while near, and the word that accomplishes its purpose.
Isa.55.world_behind: Water sellers and market cries in a dry city give the opening lines their everyday force.

deep_background.note: The word is compared to rain that does its work invisibly, drawn from dry farming rather than irrigation.

Isa.56.occasion: Sabbath welcome for foreigners and blind watchmen rebuked.
Isa.56.structure: Keep justice, foreigners and eunuchs included in the house of prayer, then a sharp rebuke of Israel's watchmen as silent dogs.
Isa.56.world_behind: Eunuchs and foreigners were barred from full assembly membership under the law, so this oracle widens the door deliberately.

deep_background.note: Later quoted by Jesus when cleansing the temple courts, which had become a market for pilgrims.

Isa.57.occasion: Idolatry rebuked and the lowly comforted.
Isa.57.structure: The righteous die unnoticed, idolatry described in detail, then the high and holy one who dwells with the contrite and heals.
Isa.57.world_behind: Child sacrifice in the valley of Hinnom is in view, a practice the prophets treat as the extreme of apostasy.

deep_background.note: Worship on hilltops under green trees was the standard Canaanite pattern the prophets condemned.

Isa.58.structure: A challenge to the loud fast, the fast God chooses described as loosing chains and feeding the hungry, then the promise of light and the sabbath.
Isa.58.world_behind: Public fasting involved bowing the head and wearing sackcloth in court squares so others would see it.

deep_background.note: Yokes bound oxen and debtors alike, so breaking the yoke covers both farm labor and debt slavery.

Isa.59.occasion: Sins separate and the Redeemer comes to Zion.
Isa.59.structure: The arm of the LORD not shortened but sin has made a wall, sins confessed in detail, no intercessor found, so God arms himself and the Redeemer comes.
Isa.59.world_behind: Armor listed piece by piece reflects real equipment: breastplate, helmet, and garments of vengeance.

deep_background.note: The gap between people and God is unfilled until God acts himself, the hinge of the passage.

Isa.60.occasion: Arise and shine, for nations stream to Zion.
Isa.60.structure: Light has come, sons and daughters return, wealth arrives by sea and camel, gates stand open always, and the city is made glorious.
Isa.60.world_behind: Gates shutting at night was basic city security, so gates never shut is a deliberate impossibility for peace.

deep_background.note: Incense and gold moved by camel from Arabia, the trade that made such wealth plausible imagery.

Isa.61.occasion: The Spirit-anointed announcement of good news.
Isa.61.structure: The speaker is anointed to preach good news to the poor, proclaim liberty, comfort mourners, then the community rejoices in its restoration.
Isa.61.world_behind: Jubilee released slaves and returned land, and the language here borrows directly from that release.

deep_background.note: A change of clothing marked a change of status, so praise replaces a spirit of heaviness like a new coat.

Isa.62.occasion: Watchmen on the walls and a new name.
Isa.62.structure: Zion will not keep silent, her new name given, watchmen appointed, and the people called the holy people, the redeemed.
Isa.62.world_behind: Watchmen were posted to spot approaching messengers, and were paid to stay awake for the city's sake.

deep_background.note: Names in Hebrew describe character, so a changed city name announces changed circumstances.

Isa.63.occasion: The warrior from Edom and the memory of mercy.
Isa.63.structure: A figure in bloodstained garments returns from Bozrah, then Israel recalls God's kindness, and the prophet appeals for the compassion of a father.
Isa.63.world_behind: Treading grapes in a winepress left red stains, the image behind the bloodied garments.

deep_background.note: The capital of Edom southeast of the Dead Sea, named here as the place of judgment.

Isa.64.occasion: A prayer for God to tear the heavens open.
Isa.64.structure: A plea for theophany, the prophet confesses that even good deeds are like filthy rags, then appeals to God as father and potter.
Isa.64.world_behind: Mountains melting at God's presence recalls Sinai, so the request is for a second Sinai, not a gentler one.

deep_background.note: Possibly a menstrual cloth, the strongest available image of uncleanness, which makes the confession total.

Isa.65.occasion: Judgment on rebels and the promise of new creation.
Isa.65.structure: God answers that he was found by those who did not seek him, judgment on apostates, then new heavens, new earth, and long life in the age to come.
Isa.65.world_behind: Eating swine flesh and sitting in tombs were ritual acts of apostasy against covenant food laws.

deep_background.note: Predator and prey diet change signals a creation restored to peace, reversing the curse.

Isa.66.occasion: The true temple and the final gathering.
Isa.66.structure: Heaven is God's throne so no house can contain him, judgment and comfort set out, and the book closes with all nations coming to worship.
Isa.66.world_behind: Temple building texts across the region claimed a deity lived in the house built for it, which this oracle denies.

deep_background.note: The pairing of new sky and new land frames the whole renewal, picked up later in the New Testament.

Isa.9.occasion: A child born and Ephraim's pride judged.
Isa.9.structure: Light to Galilee, the birth oracle with four throne names, then Jacob's arrogance indicted under four strokes of judgment.
Isa.9.world_behind: Throne names were coronation titles claimed by kings; applying four to one child claims the whole royal office.

deep_background.note: A border region hit first by Assyrian invasion, so light dawning there signals reversal from the place of earliest loss.

Isa.10.occasion: Assyria used as God's rod, then judged for its arrogance.
Isa.10.structure: Woe to unjust lawmakers, Assyria described as an axe in God's hand, its boasting indicted, then a remnant promise and the felling of the forest.
Isa.10.world_behind: Assyria's army swallowed small states by siege and deportation, which the prophet reframes as a tool God wields and then breaks.

deep_background.note: Tools do not boast against the hand that swings them, a rebuke of empire that credits itself for God's work.

Isa.11.occasion: The root of Jesse and the peaceable kingdom.
Isa.11.structure: A shoot from Jesse's stump, the sevenfold Spirit, righteous rule, Eden-like peace among animals, then the nations gathered and the highway opened.
Isa.11.world_behind: Jesse was David's father, so the stump image means the Davidic dynasty is cut down but not destroyed.

deep_background.note: Royal inscriptions boasted of cutting off a rival's dynasty; this oracle claims that cut stump sprouts again.

Isa.12.structure: Two short hymns: anger turned to comfort, then thanksgiving with the command to draw water from the wells of salvation.
Isa.12.world_behind: Water was drawn daily from wells and cisterns, making it a natural image for a supply that never runs out.

deep_background.note: Cistern water meant survival in a dry land, so the metaphor promises relief for the most routine daily need.

Isa.13.occasion: The day of the LORD against Babylon.
Isa.13.structure: An oracle summoning an army, cosmic signs, the city overthrown like Sodom, and the land left to wild animals.
Isa.13.world_behind: Babylon at this date was not yet the empire it became, so the oracle reads as the archetype of every proud city.

deep_background.note: A common prophetic term for the day God intervenes, which prophets say begins with judgment on Israel before the nations.

Isa.14.occasion: A taunt song over Babylon's king and a Philistine oracle.
Isa.14.structure: Israel restored, the tyrant mocked as fallen from heaven, Sheol stirred to meet him, then Assyria's collapse and Philistia's warning.
Isa.14.world_behind: Kings were described in hymns as climbing to divinity; the taunt reverses that royal boast step by step.

deep_background.note: Hebrew helel, rendered lucifer in Latin, named the bright planet that pales at sunrise, fitting a king whose brightness fails.

Isa.15.occasion: A lament over Moab in one night.
Isa.15.structure: Place names fall in rapid sequence, refugees flee to Zoar, water is gathered, and the prophet wails with the mourners.
Isa.15.world_behind: Moab lay east of the Dead Sea; its towns named here are the border fortresses that guarded the plateau routes.

deep_background.note: Standard mourning rites, so the prophet describes a whole country performing public grief.

Isa.16.occasion: Moab begs for refuge and its pride is humbled.
Isa.16.structure: A plea for shelter from a coming king, then God's throne established in steadfast love, followed by Moab's arrogant refusal and a three-year countdown.
Isa.16.world_behind: eastJordan's Moabites sent tribute lambs to Jerusalem, so the appeal is to a relationship already in place.

deep_background.note: Moab's wealth was sheep, so sending lambs from Sela marked submission to the Judean throne.

Isa.17.occasion: Damascus falls and Ephraim's glory fades.
Isa.17.structure: A single oracle joining Aram and northern Israel: cities emptied, harvest gleanings left, then a turn to the Maker, then sudden terror.
Isa.17.world_behind: In Damascus-Aram and Ephraim, the two northern allies pressured Judah to join an anti-Assyrian coalition, which sets the setting for Isaiah 7.

deep_background.note: Gleanings were the few olives left after harvest, the standard image of a remnant with everything stripped away.

Isa.18.occasion: Ethiopia's envoys and God's coming harvest.
Isa.18.structure: A brief oracle to a land of rivers: watch for a signal, then the LORD pruning the branches and leaving them to the birds, then gifts brought to Zion.
Isa.18.world_behind: Cush, in Nubia and modern Sudan, was a rising power that meddled in regional politics through envoys.

deep_background.note: Papyrus boats and reeds along the Nile made river travel the ordinary route between Africa and the Levant.

Isa.19.structure: The LORD rides a swift cloud, the Nile fails, counselors are confounded, then a healing turn: an altar, a highway and blessing.
Isa.19.world_behind: Egypt's economy rested entirely on the Nile flood, so striking the river attacks the nation's life source at the root.

deep_background.note: Egypt, Assyria and Israel together in one blessing was politically unthinkable and reads as the oracle's sharpest line.

Isa.20.occasion: A sign-act: Isaiah walks naked and barefoot for three years.
Isa.20.structure: A brief prose report: the LORD commands the sign, then the explanation that Egypt and Cush will be led away stripped, and Judah's allies will prove worthless.
Isa.20.world_behind: Prophets sometimes performed public sign-acts that embodied a coming event in advance.

deep_background.note: Deported prisoners were stripped as humiliation, so the prophet's own exposure enacts the exile he predicts.

Isa.21.occasion: The fall of Babylon, Dumah's question, and Arabia's fugitives.
Isa.21.structure: Three short oracles: a watchman reports the city fallen, Edom asks how long the night lasts, then a desert oracle about caravans cut off.
Isa.21.world_behind: Watchmen stood on city walls through the night, so the imagery comes directly from guard duty.

deep_background.note: Edom's question uses the night as a unit of suffering, with morning as the hoped return of relief.

Isa.22.occasion: The valley of vision and Shebna replaced by Eliakim.
Isa.22.structure: Jerusalem's festival emptied by catastrophe, then two officials contrasted: the steward deposed, the servant given keys.
Isa.22.world_behind: The royal steward carried the keys of the palace and decided access to the king's house.

deep_background.note: Household keys hung on the steward's shoulder as a sign of authority, which later supplies New Testament imagery for Christ.

Isa.23.occasion: The fall and restoration of Tyre.
Isa.23.structure: A lament from the Sea, merchants dissolved, then after seventy years the city sings again and its profit belongs to the LORD.
Isa.23.world_behind: Tyre was the Mediterranean's commercial hub, its ships trading with Egypt, Cyprus and Spain.

deep_background.note: A round number meaning a full but limited period of judgment, common in prophetic literature for exile.

Isa.24.occasion: A worldwide judgment that empties the earth.
Isa.24.structure: The LORD strips the land, the wine fails, the city is broken, the remnant sings from the ends of the earth, and the LORD of hosts reigns on Zion.
Isa.24.world_behind: Ancient cosmology pictured the earth on pillars with the sky as a curtain, so shaking the foundations means total collapse.

deep_background.note: The windows above open as in Genesis, tying the destruction back to Noah's flood.

Isa.25.occasion: Praise for victory and a feast on the mountain.
Isa.25.structure: Thanksgiving for cities overturned, then the universal banquet where death is swallowed and tears are wiped away.
Isa.25.world_behind: Victory banquets were standard royal celebration after a siege was lifted.

deep_background.note: Aged wine and rich marrow were the banquet food of the wealthy, so the promise is luxury, not bare survival.

Isa.26.occasion: A song of trust and the hope of resurrection.
Isa.26.structure: The strong city promised, the mind fixed on peace, waiting in the night, and closing with the dead rising to share the dew.
Isa.26.world_behind: Cisterns and high walls defined a defensible city, so 'strong city' invokes the practical hope of safety.

deep_background.note: Dew and resurrection are linked because dew revives parched ground overnight, an image of God's silent renewal.

Isa.27.occasion: Leviathan slain and the vineyard kept.
Isa.27.structure: The serpent dragon defeated and the vineyard kept, then Jacob cleansed and Israel gathered by trumpet blast.
Isa.27.world_behind: Returning exiles would come back from scattered lands on foot, so a distinct trumpet signal is a real rallying practice.

deep_background.note: A sea monster in Canaanite and Hebrew poetry, here simply an image of chaos power defeated by God.

Isa.28.occasion: Ephraim's drunkards judged and a cornerstone laid in Zion.
Isa.28.structure: Woe to the drunk crowns of the north, priests stagger, scoffers warned, a tested corner stone, then an illustration of a farmer's changing work.
Isa.28.world_behind: Heavy drinking was part of northern prosperity parties, and Isaiah's audience treated his warnings as baby talk.

deep_background.note: A foundation stone checked by plumb line set the alignment of a whole building, so the metaphor is about a fixed standard.

Isa.5.occasion: The song of the vineyard and six woes.
Isa.5.structure: A vineyard song that turns into a verdict, then woes against land grabbers, drunkards, mockers of God, and those who call evil good, closing with Assyria summoned.
Isa.5.world_behind: Vineyards were planted on terraced hillsides with a watchtower and a winepress cut into rock, exactly the details listed here.

deep_background.note: Hebrew beushim are literally stinking or worthless fruit, so the complaint is not bad quality but the wrong kind entirely.

Isa.6.occasion: Isaiah's vision and call in the temple.
Isa.6.structure: The throne vision with six-winged seraphim, Isaiah's uncleanness confessed and purged by a coal, then the commission with its hardening word.
Isa.6.world_behind: The temple's doorposts and the smoke place the vision in the actual building, at the moment of a king's death.

deep_background.note: Coals from the altar were used for incense, so the cleansing comes from the place of sacrifice, not a ritual bath.

Isa.7.occasion: The sign given to Ahaz during the Syro-Ephraimite crisis.
Isa.7.structure: Two kings fail to take Jerusalem, Ahaz refuses a sign, so one is given anyway: a young woman bears a son named God-with-us, and Assyria is promised.
Isa.7.world_behind: Ahaz was likely at the aqueduct checking the city's water supply during a siege threat.

deep_background.note: Food of a depopulated countryside, meaning the child will grow up in scarcity rather than abundance.

Isa.8.occasion: The sign-name scroll and the stone of stumbling.
Isa.8.structure: A name written and witnessed, Assyria described as a flood, then the command to seal the testimony and fear only the LORD.
Isa.8.world_behind: Naming a child with a sentence was a public prophetic act, with witnesses signed to the record.

deep_background.note: Binding a document and sealing it made it legally fixed until the stated time, the practice behind the instruction.

Jer.1.occasion: Jeremiah is called as a prophet in Josiah's thirteenth year.
Jer.1.structure: Call and objection, two visions, the almond branch and the boiling pot from the north.
Jer.1.world_behind: A prophet's call often came with a sign he could see; the almond wakes first in spring, and the pot tips from the north, where invasion came.

deep_background.note: The Hebrew for almond sounds like the word for watching, so a winter branch becomes a pun on God keeping his word.

Jer.2.occasion: The LORD indicts Israel for abandoning him.
Jer.2.structure: Recalled devotion at first, then the charge, then the two evils: forsaken fountain and broken cisterns.
Jer.2.world_behind: Cisterns were plastered rock chambers for rain; a cracked one held nothing, while a spring was living water.

deep_background.note: Houses depended on stored rainwater, so the image of a leaking cistern was an everyday household failure.

Jer.3.occasion: Judah is invited back despite divorce language.
Jer.3.structure: Accusation of harlotry, the call to return, then a promise of restored shepherds and a reunited land.
Jer.3.world_behind: Divorce was permitted and public; a dismissed wife could not simply return, so the invitation to come back is deliberately shocking.

deep_background.note: A written dismissal protected the woman's status, which is why its use here makes the return offer remarkable.

Jer.4.occasion: War warning sounds from the north.
Jer.4.structure: Call to return, alarm of trumpet, the lion from the thicket, then the lament over the desolation.
Jer.4.world_behind: Trumpet blasts and fleeing to walled towns were the standard response to a raiding army coming down the coastal road.

deep_background.note: Physical circumcision marked the body; the demand here is for the loyalty that mark was meant to signify.

Jer.5.occasion: Jeremiah searches Jerusalem's streets for one honest person.
Jer.5.structure: Search through the poor and the great, refusal to repent, then the coming judgment and the call to glean the remnant.
Jer.5.world_behind: Judges sat at the gate where disputes were settled, so a city with no justice at the gate had no functioning civic life.

deep_background.note: Trade and law both ran through the gate, making the gate the place where honesty was tested publicly.

Jer.6.structure: Flight urged, siege described, then the call to walk the ancient paths and the rejection of the watchmen.
Jer.6.world_behind: A besieged city was cut off from fields and wells; siege ramps and camps outside the wall are described here in detail.

deep_background.note: Roads were remembered landmarks; walking the old road meant returning to the settled ways of the ancestors.

Jer.7.occasion: Jeremiah preaches at the temple gate.
Jer.7.structure: The temple sermon: do not trust lying words, the den of robbers, then the rejection of shrine worship and the valley of slaughter.
Jer.7.world_behind: Worshipers trusted the building itself as a guarantee of safety, a conviction tied to the temple's founding promise.

deep_background.note: A robbers' cave was where stolen goods were stored safely, a picture of worship used as cover for injustice.

Jer.8.occasion: Harvest is past and the people are not saved.
Jer.8.structure: Exposure of scribes and priests, the false assurance of peace, then the harvest lament and the gathering of the remnant.
Jer.8.world_behind: Balm from Gilead was a famous resin used for wounds, so the question of why healing has not come is pointed.

deep_background.note: Gilead's resin was traded widely as medicine, making it the proverbial remedy for a wound that would not close.

Jer.9.occasion: Jeremiah weeps over the coming ruin.
Jer.9.structure: Lament over deceit, the call to weep, wisdom redefined as knowing the LORD, then the judgment on the uncircumcised.
Jer.9.world_behind: Professional mourners were hired to lead public grief, which is the practice behind the command to call the wailing women.

deep_background.note: Funerals used trained wailers to draw out communal grief, so summoning them signals a death on a national scale.

Jer.10.occasion: Idols are compared with the living God.
Jer.10.structure: Warning against the nations' customs, the carved idol as a scarecrow, then the prayer of the humbled prophet.
Jer.10.world_behind: Temple idols were dressed, carried and guarded, so a figure that cannot walk or speak is the intended contrast.

deep_background.note: A post dressed to frighten birds has no power in itself, which is exactly the comparison drawn here.

Jer.11.structure: Covenant renewal call, the plot against Jeremiah in his own town, then the plea for justice.
Jer.11.world_behind: Covenant treaties were recited aloud and bound the whole community, so breaking them was a public, not private, offense.

deep_background.note: Jeremiah's own village turned on him, showing the cost of a message the neighbours rejected.

Jer.12.occasion: Jeremiah questions why the wicked prosper.
Jer.12.structure: The prophet's complaint, God's answer about a harder race ahead, then the lament over the ruined heritage.
Jer.12.world_behind: Farmers ran races with horses only in training for war, so the answer borrows from chariot preparation.

deep_background.note: Foot soldiers were useless against chariots, so training on foot against horses meant the coming test would be worse.

Jer.13.occasion: Two sign-acts of judgment are performed.
Jer.13.structure: The linen loincloth ruined by the Euphrates, then the wineskins filled and smashed, then the warning against pride.
Jer.13.world_behind: A linen loincloth was costly undergarment cloth worn close to the body, so ruining it meant ruining what was most intimate.

deep_background.note: Babylon lay toward the Euphrates, so burying the cloth there tied the sign to the power that would take the people.

Jer.14.structure: Drought described, confession of sin, the plea not to be abandoned, then the rejection of the false prophets.
Jer.14.world_behind: Rain fed the cisterns and the grain in one season; a sustained drought emptied both food and water at once.

deep_background.note: Prophets who promised peace without a word from God traded comfort for truth, a danger named directly here.

Jer.15.occasion: The prophet is worn down by his message.
Jer.15.structure: Refusal to relent, the prophet's complaint about his birth, then God's promise to make him a fortified wall.
Jer.15.world_behind: A bronze wall was a defensive barrier in battle; being made a fortified bronze wall was a promise of survival, not comfort.

deep_background.note: The word is described as fire shut up in the bones, the classic picture of a message that cannot be suppressed.

Jer.16.occasion: Jeremiah is forbidden family life as a sign.
Jer.16.structure: No marriage or mourning, the reason given, then the promise of return from exile and the conversion of the nations.
Jer.16.world_behind: Funeral meals and mourning visits were social duties; refusing them enacted the scale of coming death.

deep_background.note: Children were the future of a household, so living without them was a living demonstration of a broken future.

Jer.17.occasion: Trust in flesh against trust in God is weighed.
Jer.17.structure: The inscribed sin, the shrub in the desert versus the tree by water, then the sabbath warning at the gate.
Jer.17.world_behind: An iron stylus cut into stone or metal; the image is of sin written permanently rather than erased.

deep_background.note: A pen of iron with a diamond point engraved lasting records, the picture of a record that does not wear off.

Jer.18.occasion: The potter's house becomes a sign.
Jer.18.structure: Watching the potter rework clay, the lesson on the nation's freedom to turn, then the plot and the prophet's cry.
Jer.18.world_behind: A potter's wheel in the Levant was a stone turntable turned by foot, with the potter reshaping a spoiled vessel by hand.

deep_background.note: Clay that failed on the wheel was kneaded back into a lump, a picture of a nation reshaped rather than discarded.

Jer.19.occasion: A clay flask is smashed outside the city.
Jer.19.structure: Purchase of the flask, the speech at Topheth, the breaking of the jar, then the return to the temple court.
Jer.19.world_behind: Topheth was the valley where refuse and child sacrifice were burned, so shattering pottery there carried a double meaning.

deep_background.note: Fired pottery cannot be repaired once shattered, unlike clay on the wheel, which is why the sign is final.

Jer.20.occasion: The prophet is beaten and put in the stocks.
Jer.20.structure: Pashhur arrests him, the name change announced, then the famous complaint about being seduced by the word.
Jer.20.world_behind: The stocks at the temple gate held a person in a fixed, humiliating posture where worshipers passed by.

deep_background.note: He tries to hold the word back and cannot, the clearest biblical picture of a compulsion to speak.

Jer.21.occasion: Zedekiah asks for a word during the siege.
Jer.21.structure: The delegation sent, the answer that the city will fall, then the choice set between life and death.
Jer.21.world_behind: Surrender to Babylon meant going out of the city, which is why the offer is framed as going out rather than staying.

deep_background.note: The options given are surrender and live or resist and die, the same choice later repeated in the final siege.

Jer.22.occasion: Judgment is pronounced on three kings.
Jer.22.structure: Charge to the royal house, then Shallum, Jehoiakim and Coniah in turn, closing with the land's lament.
Jer.22.world_behind: Kings built cedar palaces with forced labour, which is the charge brought against Jehoiakim specifically.

deep_background.note: Cedar was imported luxury timber; panelling a house in it announced wealth taken from the people.

Jer.23.occasion: False shepherds are condemned and a righteous Branch promised.
Jer.23.structure: Woe to the shepherds, the gathering of the flock, the Branch of David, then the oracle against the prophets who speak dreams.
Jer.23.world_behind: Shepherds lived with the flock and answered for strays, which is why rulers were called shepherds of the people.

deep_background.note: People mocked the prophet's message as a burden, so the phrase itself was quarrelled over and forbidden.

Jer.24.occasion: Two baskets of figs are set before the temple.
Jer.24.structure: The vision, the good figs explained as the exiles, the bad figs as those who stayed, then the promise to the exiled.
Jer.24.world_behind: Figs ripened in late summer and were pressed into cakes; early good figs were a prized delicacy and bad ones inedible.

deep_background.note: The earliest figs were the sweetest, so the exiles being called first-ripe reverses the expected verdict.

Jer.25.occasion: Seventy years of exile are declared.
Jer.25.structure: Recital of unheeded warning, the seventy years, then the cup of wrath passed to every nation in turn.
Jer.25.world_behind: A cup of wine passed around bound guests to a treaty feast, so the cup here is an obligation no one can refuse.

deep_background.note: The number matches the Babylonian supremacy remembered later by Daniel, and gave a horizon to the exile.

Jer.26.occasion: Jeremiah is tried for his temple sermon.
Jer.26.structure: The sermon repeated, the priests and prophets demand death, the elders cite precedent, then Ahikam protects him.
Jer.26.world_behind: A charge of prophesying against the temple was a capital offense, and the elders argued from a previous case with Micah.

deep_background.note: The elders saved him by citing how Micah's warning was heeded, an early appeal to legal precedent.

Jer.27.occasion: A yoke is worn as a sign to the envoys.
Jer.27.structure: The yoke made and worn, the message to the surrounding kings, then the warning against listening to diviners.
Jer.27.world_behind: A wooden yoke joined two animals at the neck; wearing one publicly announced submission without saying a word.

deep_background.note: Accepting the yoke was framed as survival, not loyalty, which made the advice politically unbearable.

Jer.28.structure: Hananiah breaks the wooden yoke, Jeremiah waits, then the word comes that iron replaces it and Hananiah dies.
Jer.28.world_behind: Prophets sometimes acted out their message with objects, so breaking a yoke was a claim to have overturned the word.

deep_background.note: Iron cannot be broken by hand, so the restated sign removes any hope of the judgment being snapped.

Jer.29.occasion: A letter is sent to the exiles in Babylon.
Jer.29.structure: Build and plant, seek the city's welfare, the seventy years, then the promise to be found when sought, plus the warning to the false prophets.
Jer.29.world_behind: Deportees were settled in communities with land, which is why the letter tells them to plant gardens and marry.

deep_background.note: Welfare of the foreign city is commanded, a stance unusual among exiles who expected quick return.

Jer.30.structure: The time of Jacob's trouble, the breaking of the yoke, the healing of the wound, then the restoration of the city.
Jer.30.world_behind: A healing wound is described with the image of an untreated injury, which in a siege became infected and fatal.

deep_background.note: A phrase later used for a final trial, here naming the destruction of the northern tribes as birth pain.

Jer.31.structure: Rachel weeping, the return of the tribes, Ephraim's repentance, then the new covenant written on the heart.
Jer.31.world_behind: Rachel's tomb stood near Ramah on the road north, where captives were assembled before deportation.

deep_background.note: Covenant law was kept on stone tablets; writing it inside a person changes where obedience comes from.

Jer.32.occasion: A field is bought while the city is under siege.
Jer.32.structure: The purchase at Anathoth with the deed sealed, the prayer of praise and doubt, then the answer that fields will be bought again.
Jer.32.world_behind: Deeds were sealed and stored in clay jars for long safekeeping, a practice attested in the Judean desert finds.

deep_background.note: Buying land under siege was economically irrational, which is precisely why it functioned as an act of hope.

Jer.33.occasion: Restoration is promised while Jeremiah is confined.
Jer.33.structure: The word comes in the court of the guard, the land restored, the Branch and the levitical promise, then the covenant with day and night.
Jer.33.world_behind: The court of the guard was a holding compound inside the palace where the prophet could still receive visitors.

deep_background.note: The regular return of day and night is used as a guarantee, an appeal to what everyone could observe.

Jer.34.occasion: A covenant to free slaves is broken.
Jer.34.structure: The siege warning to Zedekiah, the covenant of release made, then its reversal and the proclamation of liberty to the sword.
Jer.34.world_behind: Hebrew slaves were to be released in the seventh year, a rule tied to the exodus memory of being freed from Egypt.

deep_background.note: Freeing slaves during a siege reduced mouths to feed, so the reversal afterwards showed the motive was convenience.

Jer.35.occasion: The Rechabites are tested and commended.
Jer.35.structure: Wine offered in the temple chamber, their refusal, the charge to Judah, then the promise that the Rechabites will endure.
Jer.35.world_behind: The Rechabites lived as tent-dwelling herders by ancestral vow, rejecting settled farming and wine.

deep_background.note: Their obedience to a human ancestor shames a nation ignoring a divine command, the point of the comparison.

Jer.36.occasion: The scroll is written, read and burned.
Jer.36.structure: Baruch writes at dictation, the fast-day reading, the king cuts and burns it, then the scroll is rewritten with additions.
Jer.36.world_behind: Scrolls were papyrus sheets joined and rolled; cutting a column with a scribe's knife destroyed it piece by piece.

deep_background.note: Fire does not cancel a word already spoken, so the rewriting with more added shows judgment cannot be edited out.

Jer.37.occasion: The prophet is arrested as a deserter.
Jer.37.structure: Zedekiah's inquiry, the answer of surrender, the arrest at the gate, then the secret meeting and the request for bread.
Jer.37.world_behind: The Benjamin gate was the northern exit toward the prophet's home town, so his leaving looked like flight.

deep_background.note: Leaving a besieged city was treated as defection, the standard charge against those who advised surrender.

Jer.38.occasion: Jeremiah is lowered into a cistern and rescued.
Jer.38.structure: The officials demand his death, he sinks in the mud, Ebed-melech intervenes with rags, then he is drawn up and meets the king.
Jer.38.world_behind: Cisterns were bottle-shaped pits cut into rock; with the water gone they became muddy traps with no foothold.

deep_background.note: Old cloths under the armpits protected the skin, an act of practical mercy recorded in detail.

Jer.39.structure: The breach of the wall, the flight and capture of Zedekiah, the burning of the city, then the release of Jeremiah and Ebed-melech.
Jer.39.world_behind: Siege walls fell by ramp and breach; the date given matches the second month of Zedekiah's eleventh year.

deep_background.note: The prophet was kept in the palace compound, so his survival depended on his jailer as much as the victor.

Jer.40.occasion: Gedaliah governs the survivors at Mizpah.
Jer.40.structure: Jeremiah freed and given a home, Gedaliah appointed over the poor of the land, then the warning about Ishmael ignored.
Jer.40.world_behind: The poorest were left to work vineyards and fields, the standard Babylonian practice of leaving cultivators behind.

deep_background.note: Mizpah had been a gathering place for centuries, which is why it was chosen as an administrative centre.

Jer.41.structure: The assassination at the meal, the massacre of pilgrims, the flight toward Ammon, then the people turn toward Egypt.
Jer.41.world_behind: Pilgrims came with grain offerings and incense for the ruined temple, walking the road that passed Mizpah.

deep_background.note: Ammon was a rival east of the Jordan, so Ishmael's escape there shows the plot served a foreign interest.

Jer.42.occasion: The remnant asks for direction and promises obedience.
Jer.42.structure: The request made to the prophet, ten days of waiting, then the answer that they must stay in the land and not fear Babylon.
Jer.42.world_behind: Egypt offered a refuge with a long border and a strong army, which is why the survivors wanted to go there.

deep_background.note: A delayed answer tests sincerity, since the people had already decided where they wanted to go.

Jer.43.occasion: The leaders reject the answer and drag the remnant to Egypt.
Jer.43.structure: The charge of lying, the journey to Tahpanhes, then the sign of the stones hidden at Pharaoh's house.
Jer.43.world_behind: Tahpanhes was a Nile delta frontier town with a royal residence, the entry point for travellers from Judah.

deep_background.note: Burying stones under a paving and later setting a throne on them enacted Babylon's reach into Egypt itself.

Jer.44.occasion: The prophet confronts the exiles in Egypt.
Jer.44.structure: Recital of judgment on Judah, the people's defiance citing the queen of heaven, then the sign that few will return.
Jer.44.world_behind: The queen of heaven was honored with baked cakes and drink offerings, a household cult the women credited with prosperity.

deep_background.note: Bread stamped with her image was baked at home, so this was family religion rather than temple worship.

Jer.45.occasion: A personal promise is given to Baruch.
Jer.45.structure: Baruch's complaint of weariness, then the answer that his life will be preserved wherever he goes.
Jer.45.world_behind: Scribes worked closely with prophets, and a written scroll made the scribe a marked man alongside his master.

deep_background.note: The promise gives his life as plunder, meaning he keeps it the way a survivor keeps what he carried out.

Jer.46.occasion: The first oracle against the nations targets Egypt.
Jer.46.structure: Defeat at Carchemish described, the army's flight, then the word that Egypt will be punished but Jacob spared.
Jer.46.world_behind: Carchemish on the Euphrates was the crossing where Babylon broke Egypt's hold on the region in 605 BC.

deep_background.note: Egypt fielded allied troops who ran first, a detail that explains the collapse described in the poem.

Jer.47.structure: Waters rising from the north, the panic of the coastal cities, then the baldness of Gaza and Ashkelon.
Jer.47.world_behind: The Philistine plain sat on the coastal road, so any army from the north reached them before the hill country.

deep_background.note: Cutting the hair was a mourning rite, so the command to shave signals grief for a destroyed people.

Jer.48.occasion: An oracle against Moab is delivered.
Jer.48.structure: Cities taken, the god Chemosh carried off, the vineyards silenced, then the lament and the promise of restoration.
Jer.48.world_behind: Moab's plateau grew grapes and made wine, so the image of vats trodden and then silenced fits its economy.

deep_background.note: A national god captured with his people was the ultimate humiliation in ancient war propaganda.

Jer.49.occasion: Oracles address Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar and Elam.
Jer.49.structure: Five short oracles in sequence, each naming a city or people, closing with the promise of latter-day restoration for some.
Jer.49.world_behind: Edom carved rock capital and caravan routes, while Kedar herded sheep in the desert, so each oracle matches its target's livelihood.

deep_background.note: Living in rock clefts made Edom feel unassailable, which is why the oracle mocks that confidence.

Jer.50.structure: The nation from the north announced, Israel's return, then the detailed siege of Babylon and the redemption of Jacob.
Jer.50.world_behind: Babylon's canals and river gates were its defence and its weakness, a fact the later fall narrated elsewhere exploits.

deep_background.note: Babylon was devoted to Marduk, so its defeat meant its gods had failed, the same claim made against Judah's temple.

Jer.51.occasion: Babylon's judgment is spelled out at length.
Jer.51.structure: The destroying wind, the archers, the guilt for the temple's ruin, then the scroll sunk in the Euphrates as a sign.
Jer.51.world_behind: A scroll weighted and dropped into a river was a binding act, asking the heavens to witness a declared outcome.

deep_background.note: The book thrown into the Euphrates dramatises Babylon sinking, never to rise, as the text says.

Jer.52.occasion: The fall of Jerusalem is recounted as an appendix.
Jer.52.structure: Zedekiah's reign, the siege and breach, the burning of temple and city, then the release of Jehoiachin in Babylon.
Jer.52.world_behind: The temple furnishings and the bronze pillars were carried off as trophies, a detail repeated to show the scale of loss.

deep_background.note: The book ends with a prisoner seated at the king's table, a small sign of hope after total destruction.

Lam.2.occasion: The LORD's anger against Zion is described without relief.
Lam.2.structure: Acrostic: the day of wrath, the destroyed sanctuary, children fainting in the streets.
Lam.2.world_behind: Siege famine killed the weakest first, so mothers and infants dominate the imagery.

deep_background.note: The temple was called God's footstool, so its ruin meant the earth had lost its centre.

Lam.3.occasion: Personal affliction turns into the book's confession of hope.
Lam.3.structure: Grief, then the mercies that are new every morning, then a call to wait quietly.
Lam.3.world_behind: The poet speaks as a survivor of the siege, putting words to a whole city's trauma.

deep_background.note: The phrase became the anchor of Jewish morning prayer because it answers ruin with daily mercy.

Lam.4.occasion: The siege's cost is counted: hunger, gold tarnished, the anointed taken.
Lam.4.structure: Contrast between former splendour and present starvation, ending in Edom's taunt and Zion's sentence.
Lam.4.world_behind: Cannibalism in a siege is recorded in Assyrian and Babylonian siege accounts, not only here.

deep_background.note: Children were weighed as wealth; comparing them to gold measured the loss in economic terms.

Lam.5.occasion: The book closes with a prayer for restoration.
Lam.5.structure: Not acrostic: a community lament listing losses, then asking the LORD to remember and restore.
Lam.5.world_behind: The prayer names forced labour, water sold for money, and princes hanged, conditions of occupation.

deep_background.note: The final plea puts restoration entirely in God's hands, without claiming national merit.

Ezk.1.occasion: Ezekiel sees the chariot vision by the river Kebar in exile.
Ezk.1.structure: Storm wind, four living creatures, wheels within wheels, the likeness of a throne and a man.
Ezk.1.world_behind: Babylonian art used winged composite guardians, imagery a deportee would recognise at once.

deep_background.note: The vision shows God's glory outside the temple, answering the claim that exile meant abandonment.

Ezk.2.occasion: Ezekiel is commissioned to speak to a rebellious house.
Ezk.2.structure: A scroll is given and eaten, tasting sweet, then the charge to speak without fear.
Ezk.2.world_behind: Prophets were sent to a nation, not a congregation, so the commission was public and dangerous.

deep_background.note: Eating the scroll means the message is internalised before it is spoken, a picture of costly obedience.

Ezk.3.occasion: The watchman charge and a sign-act beside the exile canal.
Ezk.3.structure: Ezekiel is made a watchman, then lies on his side as a sign of the siege years.
Ezk.3.world_behind: A watchman who failed to warn a city was legally liable for the deaths, a real civic duty.

deep_background.note: The watchman's duty explains why silence is treated as guilt, not merely negligence.

Ezk.4.occasion: A clay tablet and rationed bread dramatise the coming siege.
Ezk.4.structure: Siege drawing, iron plate, barley cake baked on dung, water measured out.
Ezk.4.world_behind: Siege rations were weighed out in tiny amounts; bread baked on dung shows fuel scarcity.

deep_background.note: Cooking on human dung broke food laws, showing the siege would force uncleanness on the people.

Ezk.5.occasion: A barber's razor divides the people into three fates.
Ezk.5.structure: Shaved head and beard, a third burned, a third struck, a third scattered, a few kept.
Ezk.5.world_behind: Shaving a beard publicly shamed a man, so the sign-act humiliated the prophet as well as the nation.

deep_background.note: Famine, sword and exile are the standard curses of the covenant, listed in Leviticus 26.

Ezk.6.occasion: The mountains of Israel are addressed as the places of idolatry.
Ezk.6.structure: Judgment on the high places, then a promise that a remnant will be left.
Ezk.6.world_behind: Worship happened on raised platforms and under green trees, so the land itself was defiled.

deep_background.note: Exile did not erase identity; the remnant would remember the LORD among the nations.

Ezk.7.occasion: The end is announced with the repetition of a single word.
Ezk.7.structure: Fourfold cry that the end has come, then panic in the city and the field.
Ezk.7.world_behind: Trade stopped, silver thrown into the streets: wealth could not buy survival in a siege.

deep_background.note: The prophets' day of the LORD is first a day of judgment on Israel, not only on enemies.

Ezk.8.occasion: Ezekiel is carried in vision to the temple and shown its abominations.
Ezk.8.structure: Four scenes moving deeper into the temple, each with greater offence.
Ezk.8.world_behind: Babylonian and Egyptian cult objects in the temple courts show syncretism inside the sanctuary.

deep_background.note: Tammuz was a Mesopotamian dying god whose rites involved ritual mourning.

Ezk.9.occasion: A mark is set on the faithful before judgment falls.
Ezk.9.structure: Six executioners, a scribe with an inkhorn, a mark on the sighing, slaughter in the city.
Ezk.9.world_behind: A mark on the forehead was a protective sign, the same image used in Revelation 7.

deep_background.note: Judgment began at the sanctuary, so responsibility fell first on those who knew better.

Ezk.10.occasion: The glory of the LORD leaves the temple threshold.
Ezk.10.structure: Coals scattered over the city, the chariot wheels again, glory moving east.
Ezk.10.world_behind: The temple was the axis of the nation; its glory leaving explains why the city could fall.

deep_background.note: Fire from the altar was holy, so judgment came from the place of atonement itself.

Ezk.11.occasion: The city's leaders are judged and a new heart is promised.
Ezk.11.structure: Twenty-five officials condemned, then the promise of a heart of flesh and one spirit.
Ezk.11.world_behind: Fallen leadership who made the city a cooking pot and themselves the meat is a siege metaphor.

deep_background.note: The new heart pledge is the earliest clear statement of inward renewal by the Spirit.

Ezk.12.occasion: Ezekiel packs a bag and digs through a wall as a sign.
Ezk.12.structure: Exile sign-act, then the prince's flight through the wall, then a warning that the vision is near.
Ezk.12.world_behind: Deportation involved carrying what you could; digging through mud brick shows haste and secrecy.

deep_background.note: The people claimed the prophecy was for far off, so the prophet answered it would come now.

Ezk.13.occasion: False prophets and prophetesses are condemned.
Ezk.13.structure: Prophets who follow their own spirit, then women who hunt souls with magic bands, then the wall's fall.
Ezk.13.world_behind: Court prophets were paid to promise peace, so their words served the state rather than the truth.

deep_background.note: A wall plastered to look sound but about to collapse is the picture of a reassuring lie.

Ezk.14.occasion: Elders come with idols in their hearts and ask for a word.
Ezk.14.structure: The LORD refuses the inquiry, then names Noah, Daniel and Job as men who could save only themselves.
Ezk.14.world_behind: An inquirer kept a household idol while consulting the prophet, splitting loyalty between sources.

deep_background.note: Naming a pagan-era Daniel alongside Noah and Job shows righteousness credited across ages.

Ezk.15.occasion: Jerusalem is compared to a useless vine.
Ezk.15.structure: Vine wood has no use but fuel, and even the fire's ends are lost.
Ezk.15.world_behind: Vine wood was proverbial for being worthless when not bearing fruit, fit only for the oven.

deep_background.note: Being planted as God's vine made judgment greater, not safety greater.

Ezk.16.occasion: Israel is portrayed as an abandoned infant made a queen, then a faithless wife.
